cabanagem.s: The Cabanagem was a popular revolt in the province of Grão-Pará in the Amazon region of Brazil, lasting from 1835 to 1840. It was one of several rebellions of the Regency period and is estimated to have killed 30,000 to 40,000 people.

cacao.s: Cacao is the tree native to tropical Mesoamerica whose beans are used to make chocolate. In the Aztec Empire cacao beans were drunk by the elite as a frothy beverage and also served as a form of currency.

cadastral-survey.s: A cadastral survey is a systematic record of land parcels, recording their area, ownership, use and value, usually for taxation. The Sasanian Empire replaced a harvest-share tax with a fixed land tax based on permanent cadastral surveys of cultivated area, crop type and…

cairo.s: Cairo is a city on the Nile in Egypt, founded in 969 by the Fatimids as their capital, next to the older settlement of Fustat. It was the seat of the Fatimid Caliphate, the Ayyubid Empire and the Mamluk Sultanate, and after 1261 hosted a line of Abbasid caliphs under Mamluk…

cairo-citadel.s: The Cairo Citadel is a medieval Islamic fortress on the Muqattam hills in Cairo. It was begun by Saladin in the 1170s as part of the Ayyubid fortification of the city.

calabar.s: Calabar is a port city in southeastern Nigeria, a major centre of the Atlantic trade. After the British expedition of 1897 against the Benin Empire, Oba Ovonramwen was exiled to Calabar.

calabash.s: A calabash is a gourd dried and hollowed out for use as a container. In the Oyo Empire, the council of state, the Oyo Mesi, could reject an Alaafin by presenting him with an empty calabash, a symbol that obliged him to commit ritual suicide.

calicut.s: Calicut, now Kozhikode, is a port city on the Malabar coast of southwestern India, a major centre of the medieval spice trade. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India.

caliphate.s: A caliphate is an Islamic state ruled by a caliph, the successor to the Prophet Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community. The principal historical caliphates were the Rashidun, Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid, alongside the Almohad Caliphate in the Maghreb.

calligraphy.s: Calligraphy is the art of decorative handwriting, highly developed in the Islamic world, where it adorned manuscripts, buildings and objects. Persian calligraphy, especially the nastaliq script, was a prestigious art at Iranian courts.

calpixque.s: The calpixque (singular calpixqui) were the tribute collectors and regional administrators of the Aztec Empire. They collected tribute from subject provinces, maintained order and reported to Tenochtitlan.

calvinism.s: Calvinism is a branch of Protestant Christianity based on the teachings of John Calvin, a sixteenth-century reformer in Geneva. It spread across parts of the Holy Roman Empire, where it was recognised legally only in 1648 at the Peace of Westphalia.

cambodia.s: Cambodia is a country in mainland Southeast Asia, the heartland of the Khmer Empire, whose capital Angkor flourished between the ninth and fifteenth centuries. Its early art and religion were influenced by Indian traditions, including Gupta artistic conventions transmitted…

cambyses-ii.s: Cambyses II was the second king of the Achaemenid Empire, the son and successor of Cyrus the Great, who ruled in the late sixth century BCE. He conquered Egypt after defeating Pharaoh Psamtik III at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BCE.

camel.s: The camel is a large hoofed mammal adapted to arid environments, used for transport, milk, meat and warfare. The dromedary made long-distance caravan trade across the Sahara possible, supporting the Ghana and Almoravid empires, and was vital to Arab armies of the Rashidun…

camel-warfare.s: Camel warfare refers to the use of camels in combat, for transport of troops and supplies or as mounts. Camels' smell and appearance could unsettle horses, disrupting enemy cavalry.

cameroon.s: Cameroon is a country in west-central Africa on the Gulf of Guinea. It became a German colony in 1884 and was divided between Britain and France as a League of Nations mandate after the First World War stripped the German Empire of its colonies.

camphor.s: Camphor is a fragrant crystalline substance obtained from trees, prized in Asia as a medicine, perfume and ritual material. The finest camphor came from Sumatra and was a valuable commodity in Indian Ocean and Chinese trade.

campus-martius.s: The Campus Martius, or Field of Mars, was the annual assembly of the Frankish court, nobility and army in the Carolingian Empire, held each spring. There the ruler issued capitularies and administrative orders for the year before the army set out on campaign.

canaan.s: Canaan is the ancient name for the region of the southern Levant, roughly corresponding to present-day Israel, Palestine, Lebanon and western Syria. Its city-states were brought under Egyptian control by Thutmose III and remained a dependency of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom…

canada.s: Canada is a country in northern North America. Its eastern parts were settled as New France, the main North American colony of the French Empire, until it was conquered by Britain in the Seven Years' War and ceded in 1763.

candomble.s: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion that developed in Brazil, especially in Bahia, among enslaved Africans and their descendants. It draws heavily on Yoruba religion, including the worship of the orishas.

canton-system.s: The Canton System was the arrangement formalised by the Qing Empire in 1757 that restricted all Western maritime trade to the single port of Guangzhou, known to Europeans as Canton. Foreign merchants had to trade through licensed Chinese merchant intermediaries known as the…

cao-cao.s: Cao Cao was a Chinese warlord and statesman of the late Han period. From 196 CE he controlled the last Han emperor and dominated northern China.

cao-pi.s: Cao Pi was the son of the warlord Cao Cao and the first emperor of the Wei dynasty. In 220 CE he deposed the last Han emperor and declared his own dynasty.

cao-wei.s: Cao Wei, or the Wei dynasty, was the state founded by Cao Pi in 220 CE after he deposed the last Han emperor. It controlled northern China during the Three Kingdoms period, competing with Shu Han and Eastern Wu.

cape-colony.s: The Cape Colony was the settlement at the Cape of Good Hope established in 1652 by the Dutch East India Company as a resupply station for ships sailing to Asia. It grew into a settler colony whose descendants formed the Afrikaner community.

cape-of-good-hope.s: The Cape of Good Hope is a headland on the southwestern tip of Africa, rounded by Portuguese navigators in the late fifteenth century. The sea route around it allowed the Portuguese Empire and later the Dutch Empire to trade directly with Asia, and the VOC's monopoly covered…

cape-verde.s: Cape Verde is an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of West Africa, uninhabited until Portuguese settlement in the fifteenth century. It became an important base for Atlantic shipping and the slave trade.

capitulare-de-villis.s: The Capitulare de villis is a Carolingian capitulary, usually dated to around 800, setting out detailed rules for the management of royal estates. It specified the duties of stewards, the keeping of accounts and the crops, plants and animals to be raised.

capitulary.s: A capitulary was a legislative or administrative ordinance issued by Frankish kings, divided into chapters, or capitula. Capitularies were a principal instrument of government in the Carolingian Empire, often issued at the annual assembly.

capitulation-at-perevolochna.s: The Capitulation at Perevolochna took place in 1709 on the Dnieper River, three days after the Battle of Poltava, when the remains of the Swedish army surrendered to Russian forces. It delivered the last major Swedish field army into Russian captivity.

capitulations-of-the-ottoman-empire.s: The Capitulations were agreements by which the Ottoman Empire granted commercial and legal privileges to foreign states and their subjects. They allowed foreign merchants to trade on favourable terms and to be judged by their own consuls.

captaincies-of-brazil.s: The Captaincies of Brazil were hereditary land grants into which the Portuguese crown divided the Brazilian coast in the 1530s. Each donatary captain was responsible for settling, defending and developing his territory at private expense.

capture-of-awdaghast-992.s: The capture of Awdaghast in 992 CE was the conquest by the Ghana Empire of the oasis town of Awdaghast, previously held by Zanata Berbers. The town lay at the southern Saharan end of a major trans-Saharan gold route.

capture-of-goa.s: The capture of Goa in 1510 was the conquest of the port city on the western coast of India by Portuguese forces under Afonso de Albuquerque. Goa became the capital of the Portuguese State of India.

capture-of-hormuz-1622.s: The capture of Hormuz in 1622 was the expulsion of the Portuguese from the island fortress at the entrance of the Persian Gulf by forces of the Safavid Empire with English naval assistance. It ended more than a century of Portuguese control over Gulf trade.

capture-of-malacca-1641.s: The capture of Malacca in 1641 was the conquest of the Portuguese-held port on the Strait of Malacca by the Dutch East India Company and its Johor allies. It exemplified the Dutch strategy of seizing chokepoints of maritime trade rather than large territories.

caravan-trade.s: Caravan trade is long-distance overland commerce carried by groups of merchants with pack animals, typically camels, travelling together for safety. It linked the trans-Saharan routes of the Ghana, Mali and Kanem-Bornu empires and the Silk Road networks of the Timurid and…

caravanserai.s: A caravanserai is a roadside inn built around a courtyard, providing lodging for travellers and their animals along trade routes in the Islamic world. Caravanserais supported long-distance commerce by offering safety, storage and services.

caravel.s: A caravel was a small, highly manoeuvrable sailing ship developed by the Portuguese in the fifteenth century, often with lateen sails that allowed it to sail close to the wind. It was used in voyages of exploration along the African coast.

caribbean.s: The Caribbean is the region of islands and coasts surrounding the Caribbean Sea, colonised by European powers from the late fifteenth century. Its plantation economies, worked by enslaved Africans, many from regions such as Kongo, made it a centre of the Spanish, British and…

carloman-i.s: Carloman I was a Frankish king, the son of Pepin the Short and the brother of Charlemagne, with whom he shared the kingdom from 768. Relations between the brothers were tense.

carnation-revolution.s: The Carnation Revolution was a largely bloodless military coup in Lisbon on 25 April 1974 that overthrew the Estado Novo dictatorship in Portugal. Its leaders were partly motivated by the costly colonial wars in Africa.

carolingian-empire.s: The Carolingian Empire was the Frankish realm ruled by the Carolingian dynasty, reaching its height under Charlemagne, who was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. It covered much of western and central Europe and fostered the Carolingian Renaissance.

carolingian-minuscule.s: Carolingian minuscule is a clear, legible script developed in the late eighth century in the Carolingian Empire. It was used to copy classical and religious texts in monastic scriptoria during the Carolingian Renaissance.

carolingian-renaissance.s: The Carolingian Renaissance was a revival of learning, literature and the arts in the Carolingian Empire in the late eighth and ninth centuries. Led by scholars such as Alcuin at the court of Charlemagne, it promoted education, church reform and the copying of classical and…

carrack.s: A carrack was a large, three- or four-masted ocean-going sailing ship developed in the Mediterranean and Iberia in the fifteenth century. Its size allowed it to carry large cargoes and defend itself on long voyages.

carthage.s: Carthage was a Phoenician city founded on the coast of present-day Tunisia, traditionally in the ninth century BCE, which became the capital of the Punic Empire. It dominated trade in the western Mediterranean and fought three Punic Wars with Rome, which destroyed it in 146 BCE.

carthago-delenda-est.s: Carthago delenda est, "Carthage must be destroyed", is a Latin phrase associated with the Roman senator Cato the Elder, who is said to have ended his speeches with it. It expresses Roman hostility to Carthage in the years before the Third Punic War.

cartography.s: Cartography is the science and art of making maps. Portuguese navigators of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries greatly expanded European geographical knowledge and charts of Africa and Asia.

casa-da-india.s: The Casa da Índia was the royal trading house in Lisbon that managed the crown monopoly over spice imports from Asia in the sixteenth century. It organised fleets, collected goods and redistributed them to European markets.

casa-de-contratacion.s: The Casa de Contratación, or House of Trade, was the Spanish crown agency founded in Seville in 1503 to regulate trade and navigation with the Americas. It licensed voyages, collected duties and trained pilots.

caspian-sea.s: The Caspian Sea is the world's largest inland body of water, between the Caucasus, Iran and Central Asia. Its northern shores were the base of the Khazar Khaganate, and its southern shores formed part of the Seljuk and Safavid empires.

cassander.s: Cassander was a Macedonian general and ruler of Macedonia after the death of Alexander the Great, one of the Diadochi who fought over Alexander's empire. He joined Ptolemy and Lysimachus in a coalition against Antigonus I.

cassava.s: Cassava, also called manioc, is a starchy root crop native to South America. Carried across the Atlantic as part of the Columbian Exchange promoted by the Spanish Empire and other colonial powers, it became a staple food in Africa.

caste.s: Caste refers to a system of hereditary social groups, often tied to occupation and restricting marriage between groups. In the Jolof Empire, Wolof society distinguished nobles, free commoners, artisan castes such as blacksmiths and griots, and enslaved people.

castrum.s: A castrum (plural castra) was a Roman military camp or fortress, laid out on a standard rectangular plan with gates and intersecting main streets. Permanent castra housed the legions along the frontiers of the Roman Empire.

cataphract.s: A cataphract was a heavily armoured cavalryman, with both rider and horse protected by armour, who charged with a long lance. Cataphracts were a principal component of the army of the Parthian Empire, alongside highly mobile horse archers.

catapult.s: A catapult is a siege engine that hurls projectiles using tension, torsion or human traction, used before gunpowder artillery. Chinese armies of the Song Dynasty used traction catapults extensively in siege warfare.

cataract-surgery.s: Cataract surgery is the treatment of the clouding of the eye's lens. In ancient India, the surgical compendium attributed to the physician Sushruta described a technique of couching the cataract.

catherine-the-great.s: Catherine the Great, or Catherine II, was empress of Russia from 1762 to 1796. Her reign saw major territorial expansion, including gains on the Black Sea coast and Crimea from the Ottomans.

catholic-league.s: The Catholic League was an alliance of Catholic states of the Holy Roman Empire formed in 1609, led by Bavaria, which fought on the imperial side in the Thirty Years' War. Its army under Tilly won major victories in the early phase of the war.

catholicism.s: Catholicism is the faith and practice of the Roman Catholic Church, headed by the pope in Rome. It was the official religion of the Spanish Empire and of most of the Holy Roman Empire, and the faith of the majority in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

cato-the-elder.s: Cato the Elder was a Roman statesman and writer of the second century BCE, famous for his conservatism and moral severity. He is remembered for ending his speeches with the declaration that Carthage must be destroyed.

cattle.s: Cattle are domesticated bovines kept for milk, meat, hides and draught, and in many societies as a measure of wealth. Herds were central to the economies and social structures of the Mutapa and Rozvi empires, whose founder Changamire Dombo began as a cattle administrator, and…

caucasus.s: The Caucasus is the mountainous region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, lying between Europe and Asia. It was contested for centuries by successive powers, including the Khazar Khaganate, the Seljuk Empire and the Afsharid Empire.

cavalry-warfare.s: Cavalry warfare is the use of mounted troops in battle, for shock charges, archery, scouting and rapid pursuit. Mounted mobility gave a recurring advantage to states that could breed horses and train riders, allowing swift conquest of large territories and domination of…

cayor.s: Cayor was a Wolof kingdom in what is now western Senegal, one of the constituent states of the Jolof Empire. As Atlantic trade expanded in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Cayor gained direct access to European goods and revenues.

censorate.s: The Censorate was a Chinese government agency responsible for monitoring the conduct of officials and reporting misconduct to the emperor. Its origins lie in the supervisory offices of the Han Dynasty.

census.s: A census is an official count of a population, often recording households, property and obligations. Censuses enabled states to assess taxes and military service, as in the Roman Empire and the record-keeping of the Macedonian and Seleucid empires.

central-africa.s: Central Africa is the region of the African continent centred on the Congo basin, including present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Congo, Angola and neighbouring countries. It was home to the Kongo Empire near the Atlantic coast and the Lunda Empire in…

central-african-republic.s: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country in central Africa, formerly the French colony of Ubangi-Shari. Its northern regions bordered the Wadai Empire, which raided them for slaves.

central-asia.s: Central Asia is the vast inland region between the Caspian Sea and western China, including the steppes and the oasis cities of Transoxiana such as Samarkand and Bukhara. It was a crossroads of the Silk Road and the homeland or battleground of many empires, from the Achaemenid…

central-bank.s: A central bank is a public institution that manages a state's currency, money supply and banking system. Sweden's Riksbank, founded in 1668, is generally considered the oldest central bank still in operation.

central-europe.s: Central Europe is the region between Western and Eastern Europe, broadly including Germany, Austria, the Czech lands, Poland and Hungary. In the early medieval period its western parts lay within the Carolingian Empire.

central-powers.s: The Central Powers were the coalition of Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria that fought against the Allies in the First World War. Their defeat in 1918 led to the collapse of all four monarchies.

central-sudan.s: The central Sudan is the part of the Sahel and savanna belt of West and Central Africa between the Niger bend and Lake Chad, in the historical sense of the Bilad al-Sudan. It was the home of the Hausa city-states and of Kanem-Bornu.

ceuta.s: Ceuta is a port city on the North African coast opposite Gibraltar. Its conquest by King João I of Portugal and his sons, including Prince Henry the Navigator, in 1415 initiated the Portuguese Empire's overseas expansion.

ceylon.s: Ceylon is the former name of Sri Lanka, an island south of India famous for cinnamon. Its coastal areas were controlled by the Portuguese Empire in the sixteenth century and then taken by the Dutch Empire in the seventeenth century.

chad.s: Chad is a landlocked country in north-central Africa named after Lake Chad. The region around Lake Chad was the heartland of the Kanem-Bornu Empire, while the east was the home of the Wadai Empire.

chagatai-khan.s: Chagatai Khan was the second son of Genghis Khan, who received a share of the Mongol Empire in Central Asia and ruled from 1227 to 1242. His territories included Transoxiana, the Ili River valley and the Tarim Basin, formerly ruled by the Qara Khitai.

chagatai-khanate.s: The Chagatai Khanate was the Mongol successor state in Central Asia ruled by the descendants of Chagatai Khan from the thirteenth century. It covered Transoxiana and the lands east to the Tarim Basin and gradually adopted Islam.

chagatai-language.s: Chagatai is an extinct Turkic literary language of Central Asia, named after the Chagatai Khanate. It flourished under the Timurid Empire, especially in the works of the poet Ali-Shir Nava'i.

chaghri-beg.s: Chaghri Beg was a grandson of Seljuk and brother of Tughril, with whom he led the Seljuk Turks in the early eleventh century. The brothers captured Merv and Nishapur and defeated the Ghaznavids at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040.

chain-mail.s: Chain mail is armour made of small interlocking metal rings. In the Sokoto Caliphate, some emirates fielded armoured horsemen equipped in a tradition of quilted and chain-mail armour long characteristic of Sudanic warfare.

chaldean-empire.s: The Chaldean Empire, also known as the Neo-Babylonian Empire, was a Mesopotamian state centred on Babylon, founded in 626 BCE by Nabopolassar. Allied with the Medes, it destroyed Assyria and under Nebuchadnezzar II dominated the Near East and rebuilt Babylon.

chaldean-tribes.s: The Chaldean tribes were Semitic-speaking peoples who settled in southern Mesopotamia in the early first millennium BCE. They frequently resisted the Assyrian Empire's control of Babylonia.

cham.s: The Cham are a people of Southeast Asia whose kingdom of Champa occupied the central and southern coast of present-day Vietnam. They were long-standing rivals of the Khmer Empire, with which they fought repeated wars.

cham-sack-of-angkor.s: The Cham sack of Angkor occurred in 1177, when forces of the kingdom of Champa captured and plundered the capital of the Khmer Empire. The attack exposed the empire's vulnerabilities.

champa.s: Champa was a group of kingdoms of the Cham people on the central and southern coast of present-day Vietnam, from the early centuries CE until absorbed by Vietnam. It was a maritime trading power linked to China and India.

champa-rice.s: Champa rice refers to fast-ripening, drought-resistant rice varieties introduced to China from Champa in present-day Vietnam. The Song Dynasty promoted them in the early eleventh century.

chanakya.s: Chanakya, also known as Kautilya, was an ancient Indian scholar and statesman traditionally regarded as the chief adviser to Chandragupta Maurya. He is credited with the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economics and military strategy.

chandragupta-i.s: Chandragupta I was the ruler who established the Gupta Empire as a major power in northern India around 320 CE. He took the title of maharajadhiraja and strengthened his position through marriage to a Licchavi princess.

chandragupta-ii.s: Chandragupta II, also called Vikramaditya, was a ruler of the Gupta Empire who reigned from about 375 to 415 CE. He extended the empire to western India by defeating the Western Kshatrapas.

chandragupta-maurya.s: Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Maurya Empire, which he established in 321 BCE after overthrowing the Nanda dynasty, traditionally with the help of Chanakya. He extended his rule across northern India and fought Seleucus I, gaining territories in the northwest in…

changamire.s: Changamire was the title of the rulers of the Rozvi Empire on the Zimbabwe plateau, taken from the founder Changamire Dombo. The title had earlier been associated with a powerful figure within the Mutapa state.

changamire-dombo.s: Changamire Dombo was the founder of the Rozvi Empire on the Zimbabwe plateau in the late seventeenth century. He began as a cattle administrator under the Mutapa ruler Mukombwe before breaking with him.

changan.s: Chang'an, now Xi'an, is a city in the Wei River valley of northwestern China, the capital of several dynasties including the Han and Tang. Under the Tang Dynasty it was one of the largest and most cosmopolitan cities in the world, the eastern terminus of the Silk Road.

chanyu.s: Chanyu was the title of the supreme ruler of the Xiongnu Empire, roughly equivalent to emperor. The chanyu presided over a hierarchy of kings and tribal leaders and conducted relations with Han China.

chanyuan-treaty.s: The Chanyuan Treaty was a peace agreement concluded in 1005 between the Song Dynasty and the Khitan Liao dynasty. The Song agreed to pay annual tribute in silver and silk in return for peace along the northern frontier.

chao-currency.s: Chao was the paper currency issued by the Yuan Dynasty in China. The Yuan made paper money the main medium of exchange throughout its realm, a system described with astonishment by Marco Polo.

charcoal.s: Charcoal is a fuel produced by heating wood in the absence of air, and was essential for smelting iron in the pre-industrial world. The Kushite region around Meroë became a centre of iron production, facilitated by abundant wood for charcoal.

chariot.s: A chariot is a light, two-wheeled, horse-drawn vehicle used in warfare, carrying a driver and an archer or spearman. Chariots were decisive weapons in the Late Bronze Age, used by the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, the Hittite Empire and the Mitanni Empire, renowned for their…

charlemagne.s: Charlemagne was king of the Franks from 768 and was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope Leo III in 800. He conquered much of western and central Europe, including Saxony and Lombard Italy, and promoted the Carolingian Renaissance.

charles-de-gaulle.s: Charles de Gaulle was a French general and statesman who led the Free French during the Second World War and later founded the Fifth Republic, serving as president from 1959 to 1969. Free French forces relied heavily on France's African colonies.

charles-iv.s: Charles IV was Holy Roman Emperor in the fourteenth century and king of Bohemia, ruling from Prague. In 1356 he issued the Golden Bull, which codified the election of the emperor by seven electors.

charles-maccarthy.s: Sir Charles MacCarthy was a British colonial governor of Sierra Leone and the Gold Coast settlements in the early nineteenth century. He led a British expedition against the Ashanti Empire and was killed at the Battle of Nsamankow in 1824, when his force was annihilated.

charles-martel.s: Charles Martel was a Frankish military leader and mayor of the palace who effectively ruled the Frankish kingdom in the early eighth century. He defeated an Umayyad army at the Battle of Tours in 732 CE.

charles-the-fat.s: Charles the Fat was a Carolingian ruler who briefly reunited the realms of the Carolingian Empire between 881 and 888 CE. His reign was undermined when he paid tribute to the Vikings besieging Paris rather than fight them.

charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.s: Charles V was a Habsburg ruler who became king of Spain as Charles I in 1516 and Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. He inherited the Spanish, Burgundian and Habsburg lands, presiding over the Spanish conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires.

charles-x-gustav.s: Charles X Gustav was king of Sweden in the mid-seventeenth century and a gifted military commander. After a daring winter crossing of the frozen straits between Danish islands, he forced Denmark to accept the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658.

charles-xi-of-sweden.s: Charles XI was king of Sweden in the late seventeenth century. He strengthened royal power, reclaimed alienated crown lands from the nobility in the Great Reduction and reformed state finances.

charles-xii-of-sweden.s: Charles XII was king of Sweden from 1697 to 1718 and a commander of great tactical skill. He won notable victories such as Narva in 1700 but was decisively defeated by Peter I of the Russian Empire at Poltava in 1709, after which he spent years in Ottoman exile.

charter-oath.s: The Charter Oath was a statement of five principles promulgated in 1868 at the start of the Meiji era in Japan in the name of the young emperor. It promised deliberative assemblies, the participation of all classes, the abandonment of outdated customs and the seeking of…

chartered-company.s: A chartered company was a trading enterprise granted a charter by a state giving it monopoly rights and often governmental powers, such as making war and administering territory. Such companies were key instruments of early modern European expansion, including the Dutch and…

chauth.s: Chauth was a levy of one quarter of the land revenue, collected by the Marathas from territories outside their direct rule. Paying chauth secured a region against Maratha raids.

chemical-weapons.s: Chemical weapons are toxic substances used in war to kill or injure, such as mustard gas. They were used on a large scale in the First World War and later banned by international agreement.

chenab.s: The Chenab is a river rising in the Himalayas and flowing through Jammu and Kashmir and the Punjab, one of the five rivers that give the Punjab its name. It joins the other Punjab rivers before reaching the Indus.

chenqiao-mutiny.s: The Chenqiao Mutiny was the coup of 960 CE in which troops of the Later Zhou commander Zhao Kuangyin draped him in the imperial yellow robe and proclaimed him emperor. Zhao took the reign name Taizu.

chernigov.s: Chernigov, now Chernihiv, is a historic city in northern Ukraine, one of the oldest towns of Kievan Rus. The Truce of Deulino in 1618 confirmed Polish possession of Smolensk and Chernigov.

chernozem.s: Chernozem, or black earth, is a highly fertile dark soil rich in humus, found across the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia. Its grain yields made the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth a breadbasket of early modern Europe, exporting grain through the Baltic.

chewa.s: The chewa were professional military regiments in the Ethiopian Empire. Emperor Amda Seyon I, who acceded in 1314, restructured the army around these regiments.

chhatrapati.s: Chhatrapati was the royal title adopted by Shivaji at his coronation in 1674, meaning lord of the parasol, a symbol of sovereignty. It was held by Shivaji and his successors as rulers of the Maratha state.

chiapas.s: Chiapas is a state in southern Mexico, bordering Guatemala. Under Ahuitzotl, the Aztec Empire extended its conquests south to Xoconusco, the Pacific coastal region of modern Chiapas.

chibinda-ilunga.s: Chibinda Ilunga is a legendary Luba prince and hunter traditionally credited with marrying into the Lunda royal line, in the person of the female ruler Lueji. He is said to have introduced the Luba model of sacred kingship and administration.

chihalgani.s: The Chihalgani, or Council of Forty, was a group of powerful Turkic slave nobles in the Delhi Sultanate during the thirteenth century, associated with Sultan Iltutmish. They dominated court politics and made and unmade sultans after his death.

child-sacrifice.s: Child sacrifice refers to the ritual killing of children as offerings to deities. Ancient Greek and Roman writers accused the Carthaginians of sacrificing children to Baal Hammon, and the tophet burial grounds of Carthage contain the remains of many infants.

chimalpopoca.s: Chimalpopoca was the third ruler of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan in the early fifteenth century, when they were tributaries of the Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco. During the succession struggle after the death of the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc in 1426, he was allegedly murdered on…

china.s: China is a country in East Asia, home to one of the world's oldest continuous civilisations, unified under successive dynasties including the Han, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing. Its silk, porcelain and other goods drew trade across the Silk Road and the Indian Ocean, linking…

chinampa.s: A chinampa is an artificial agricultural plot built up from mud and vegetation in shallow lake beds, separated by canals. The chinampas of the Valley of Mexico produced several harvests a year.

chirisamhuru-ii.s: Chirisamhuru II was the last Changamire ruler of the Rozvi Empire. The Rozvi state was weakened in the early nineteenth century by invasions of Nguni groups from the south during the Mfecane.

chirisamuru.s: Chirisamuru was a Changamire ruler of the Rozvi Empire whose reign the site dates to about 1712 to 1788. During this long reign the Rozvi military mainly served as a deterrent against Portuguese attempts to re-establish inland footholds.

chogha-zanbil.s: Chogha Zanbil is an archaeological site in southwestern Iran containing one of the best-preserved ziggurats in the world. It was built around 1340 BCE by King Untash-Napirisha as a religious complex.

chokwe.s: The Chokwe are a people of present-day northeastern Angola and the southern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Skilled hunters and traders, they expanded in the nineteenth century through the trade in ivory, wax and rubber.

chola-empire.s: The Chola Empire was a Tamil dynasty of southern India that reached its height in the eleventh century. It built a powerful navy and extended its influence across the Bay of Bengal.

chola-invasion-of-srivijaya.s: The Chola invasion of Srivijaya refers to naval raids launched by the Chola Empire of southern India against Srivijaya's ports in 1025, under Rajendra I, and again around 1068. The raids sacked several Srivijayan centres and seized the ruler.

chonin.s: The chonin were the townspeople of Edo-period Japan, mainly merchants and artisans. Officially ranked below samurai and peasants in the Tokugawa Shogunate's social hierarchy, they grew wealthy through commerce in cities such as Edo and Osaka.

choshu-domain.s: Choshu was a feudal domain in western Japan, ruled by the Mori family. With Satsuma, it led the opposition to the Tokugawa Shogunate in the 1860s.

christianity.s: Christianity is a monotheistic religion based on the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth, which arose in the first century CE. It became the state religion of the Roman and Byzantine empires and of the Aksumite and Ethiopian empires, and was spread by the Carolingian,…

christina-queen-of-sweden.s: Christina was queen of Sweden, succeeding her father Gustavus Adolphus as a child in 1632. During her minority, which lasted to 1644, the chancellor Axel Oxenstierna governed and built a sophisticated central administration of collegiate boards.

christopher-columbus.s: Christopher Columbus was a Genoese navigator whose voyage of 1492, funded by the Castilian crown, reached the Caribbean. His voyages initiated Spanish colonisation of the Americas and the rise of the Spanish Empire.

chu-han-contention.s: The Chu-Han Contention was the civil war that followed the collapse of the Qin dynasty in the late third century BCE, fought between Xiang Yu of Chu and Liu Bang of Han. Liu Bang emerged victorious and proclaimed himself emperor.

chupan.s: Chupan was a powerful Mongol military commander, or amir, in the Ilkhanate in the early fourteenth century. He held effective power during the minority of Abu Sa'id, who came to the throne in 1317.

chupanids.s: The Chupanids were a dynasty descended from the Mongol commander Chupan that controlled parts of northwestern Iran and Azerbaijan in the mid-fourteenth century. They emerged as one of the rival regional powers after the death of Abu Sa'id in 1335.

church-of-the-east.s: The Church of the East is an ancient Christian church centred in Mesopotamia, often called Nestorian. Its missionaries spread its faith across Central Asia to China.

cilicia.s: Cilicia is a historical region on the southeastern coast of Anatolia, north of Cyprus. It controlled routes between Anatolia and Syria through the Cilician Gates.

cinnamon.s: Cinnamon is a spice made from the inner bark of trees of the genus Cinnamomum, the finest coming from Sri Lanka. It was one of the most valuable commodities of the Asian spice trade.

cisleithania.s: Cisleithania was the unofficial name of the Austrian half of the Austro-Hungarian Empire after the Compromise of 1867, named after the Leitha River that formed part of the border with Hungary. It included Austria, Bohemia, Moravia, Galicia, Dalmatia and other lands.

cisplatine-war.s: The Cisplatine War was fought from 1825 to 1828 between the Brazilian Empire and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata over the Cisplatine Province, present-day Uruguay. The war was costly and unpopular in Brazil.

civil-disobedience.s: Civil disobedience is the deliberate, non-violent refusal to obey certain laws or government demands as a form of political protest. It was used on a mass scale by Mahatma Gandhi's Indian National Congress movement against British rule.

civil-law.s: Civil law is a legal tradition based on comprehensive written codes, derived ultimately from Roman law. Its foundations lie in the law of the Roman Empire and the Corpus Juris Civilis compiled in the Byzantine Empire.

civil-war.s: Civil war, armed conflict between rival factions within a single state, is a recurring cause of imperial decline. Succession disputes, regional rebellions and rivalry among generals drained resources, divided armies and invited foreign intervention.

claude-auguste-court.s: Claude-Auguste Court was a French soldier who served Maharaja Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire in the 1820s and 1830s. He was one of several European officers, veterans of the Napoleonic armies, employed to modernise the Sikh army.

claudius-ptolemy.s: Claudius Ptolemy was a Greek mathematician, astronomer and geographer who worked in Alexandria in the second century CE. His Almagest and Geography were the leading authorities in their fields for over a millennium.

cleopatra-vii.s: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Empire, reigning from 51 to 30 BCE. She allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony in an attempt to preserve Egypt's independence.

closure-of-the-neoplatonic-academy.s: The closure of the Neoplatonic Academy refers to the Byzantine emperor Justinian's measures in 529 CE that ended pagan philosophical teaching in Athens. Several of the displaced philosophers travelled to the court of the Sasanian king Khosrow I.

cloves.s: Cloves are the aromatic dried flower buds of a tree native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia. They were among the most valuable spices of the Asian trade.

clovis-i.s: Clovis I was king of the Franks in the late fifth and early sixth centuries and founder of the Merovingian dynasty. He united most of the Frankish tribes, conquered much of Gaul and converted to Catholic Christianity.

coal.s: Coal is a combustible sedimentary rock used as fuel. Under the Song Dynasty, coal was used on a large scale in iron smelting and urban heating.

code-of-hammurabi.s: The Code of Hammurabi is a Babylonian law code issued around 1754 BCE by Hammurabi, king of the Babylonian Empire, inscribed on a basalt stele. It contains nearly 300 laws on commerce, property, family and crime, including the principle of proportional punishment.

code-of-ur-nammu.s: The Code of Ur-Nammu is the oldest known surviving law code, issued in the Third Dynasty of Ur by Ur-Nammu or his son Shulgi. Written in Sumerian, it prescribed monetary fines for many offences.

codex-justinianus.s: The Codex Justinianus is the collection of imperial Roman laws compiled on the orders of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I in the sixth century CE. It formed one part of the larger Corpus Juris Civilis.

coele-syria.s: Coele-Syria, meaning "hollow Syria", was the name used in the Hellenistic period for the southern Levant, including Phoenicia and Palestine. It was disputed between the Ptolemaic Empire and the Seleucid Empire in a series of Syrian Wars.

coffee-economy.s: Coffee is a drink made from the roasted seeds of the coffee plant, originally from Ethiopia and Yemen, which spread through the Islamic world and then Europe. Coffee became the dominant export of the Brazilian Empire, cultivated by enslaved labour, and a plantation crop in…

cohong.s: The Cohong was the guild of licensed Chinese merchants at Guangzhou through which all Western maritime trade was conducted under the Canton System of the Qing Empire. The merchants were responsible for the conduct of foreign traders and the payment of duties.

cohort.s: A cohort was a tactical unit of the Roman army, normally about 480 men, with ten cohorts forming a legion. It became the main manoeuvre unit of the Roman Empire's legions.

collegium-russia.s: The collegia were administrative boards created in Russia by Peter I in 1718, each responsible for a branch of government such as foreign affairs, war or finance. The system was inspired by Swedish models.

collegium-sweden.s: The collegia were central administrative boards created in Sweden under the chancellor Axel Oxenstierna, responsible for finance, war, admiralty, justice and commerce. They were organised during the minority of Queen Christina.

colmar.s: Colmar is a town in Alsace, in eastern France. Near it, in 833 CE, the army of Louis the Pious deserted to his rebellious sons, an episode known as the "Field of Lies".

cologne.s: Cologne is a city on the Rhine in western Germany, founded as a Roman colony and an important centre of the Roman Empire's Rhine frontier. In the Middle Ages its archbishop was one of the seven electors of the Holy Roman Empire.

colonel-moll.s: Colonel Moll was a French colonial officer who commanded French forces in the region of present-day Chad. In June 1909 his force defeated the Wadai army at the Battle of Abéché and captured the capital.

columbia-university.s: Columbia University is a private research university in New York City, founded in 1754. It has been a major centre for the study of Japanese history and culture.

columbian-exchange.s: The Columbian Exchange is the transfer of plants, animals, diseases and people between the Americas and the rest of the world following Columbus's voyages from 1492. American crops such as maize, potatoes and cassava transformed nutrition worldwide, while Old World diseases…

commander-of-the-faithful.s: Commander of the Faithful, in Arabic Amir al-Mu'minin, is a title of the caliph as supreme leader of the Muslim community. The Abbasid caliphs used it to express their dual religious and political authority.

commandery.s: A commandery was a large administrative unit of imperial China, divided into counties and governed by officials appointed by the central government. The system originated under the Qin and was extended by the Han Dynasty.

common-law.s: Common law is a legal system developed in England, based largely on judicial precedent and court decisions rather than comprehensive written codes. The British Empire spread it to its colonies, and it underlies the legal systems of many countries today.

commonwealth-of-nations.s: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of independent states, most of them former territories of the British Empire. It evolved from the self-governing dominions of the empire in the first half of the twentieth century.

companion-cavalry.s: The Companion cavalry, or hetairoi, was the elite heavy cavalry of the Macedonian army, recruited from the Macedonian aristocracy. Under Alexander the Great it delivered the decisive charges at battles such as Gaugamela.

composite-bow.s: A composite bow is a bow made from layers of wood, horn and sinew glued together, giving great power in a short length suitable for use on horseback. It was the principal weapon of steppe and Iranian horse archers.

concentration-camp.s: A concentration camp is a place where large numbers of civilians or prisoners are detained, usually without trial, in harsh conditions. During the Second Boer War of 1899–1902, the British army interned Boer women and children and black Africans in camps where many thousands…

concert-of-europe.s: The Concert of Europe was the system of cooperation among the great powers of Europe established after the Congress of Vienna in 1815, aiming to preserve the balance of power and prevent revolution. The Russian Empire was one of its five great powers.

confederation-of-the-equator.s: The Confederation of the Equator was a short-lived republican and separatist revolt in northeastern Brazil in 1824, centred on Pernambuco. It arose in opposition to Emperor Pedro I's centralising constitution.

confederation-of-the-rhine.s: The Confederation of the Rhine was a union of German states formed in 1806 under the protection of Napoleon. Its creation led Francis II to abdicate the imperial title later that year.

confucianism.s: Confucianism is a system of ethical, social and political thought based on the teachings of Confucius, a Chinese philosopher of the fifth century BCE. It stresses hierarchy, filial piety, benevolent government and education.

congo-basin.s: The Congo basin is the vast drainage area of the Congo River in Central Africa, largely covered by tropical rainforest. Its southern savanna fringes were the home of the Luba and Lunda states.

congo-free-state.s: The Congo Free State was a state in Central Africa controlled personally by King Leopold II of Belgium from 1885 to 1908. Its regime of forced labour, especially for rubber collection, caused immense suffering.

congo-river.s: The Congo River is the second longest river in Africa, flowing through Central Africa to the Atlantic. The Kingdom of Kongo occupied the lands south of its lower course.

congress-of-vienna.s: The Congress of Vienna was a conference of European powers held in 1814–1815 to reorganise Europe after the Napoleonic Wars. Alexander I played a dominant role, establishing the Russian Empire as one of the five great powers.

congreve-rocket.s: The Congreve rocket was a British military rocket developed by William Congreve in the early nineteenth century, based on rockets used in Mysore. It was inaccurate but had a strong psychological effect.

conquest-of-ceuta.s: The conquest of Ceuta was the capture of the Muslim port on the North African coast by Portuguese forces under King João I and his sons, including Prince Henry, in 1415. It initiated the overseas expansion of the Portuguese Empire.

conquest-of-larsa.s: The conquest of Larsa was Hammurabi's capture of the rival southern Mesopotamian kingdom of Larsa, ruled by Rim-Sin, in 1762 BCE. Larsa had been one of the leading powers of the region.

conscription.s: Conscription is compulsory enlistment of people into state service, especially the armed forces. Ancient states such as the Han Dynasty and the Hittite Empire relied on obligatory military service, and the Tang Dynasty had its militia system.

conservative-party-brazil.s: The Conservative Party was one of the two main political parties of the Brazilian Empire, alongside the Liberal Party. It favoured a strong central government and the monarchy.

constantine-i.s: Constantine I, known as Constantine the Great, was Roman emperor in the early fourth century CE. He was the first emperor to convert to Christianity and legalised the faith throughout the Roman Empire.

constantine-xi-palaiologos.s: Constantine XI Palaiologos was the last emperor of the Byzantine Empire. He died in 1453 defending Constantinople against the Ottoman army of Mehmed II.

constantinople.s: Constantinople, now Istanbul, was the city on the Bosphorus refounded by Constantine I in the fourth century CE on the site of Byzantion. It was the capital of the Byzantine Empire for over a thousand years and one of the largest and richest cities of the medieval world,…

constantius-ii.s: Constantius II was a Roman emperor of the fourth century CE, a son of Constantine I. He fought prolonged wars on the eastern frontier against the Sasanian king Shapur II.

constitutio-antoniniana.s: The Constitutio Antoniniana, also called the Edict of Caracalla, was a decree issued by the Roman emperor Caracalla in 212 CE. It granted Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the Roman Empire.

constitution-of-3-may-1791.s: The Constitution of 3 May 1791 was a reforming constitution adopted by the Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. It was the first modern written constitution in Europe, abolishing the liberum veto and strengthening the monarchy.

constitution-of-japan.s: The Constitution of Japan was adopted in 1947 under the Allied occupation after the Second World War, replacing the Meiji Constitution of 1889. It made the emperor a symbol of the state with no political power and established popular sovereignty.

constitutional-monarchy.s: A constitutional monarchy is a form of government in which a monarch is head of state but exercises power within the limits of a constitution. The Brazilian Empire under its 1824 constitution and the Empire of Japan under the Meiji Constitution of 1889 were constitutional…

consul.s: A consul was the highest elected magistrate of the Roman Republic, two being elected annually to command armies and preside over the government. Under the Roman Empire the office survived as a prestigious honour without real power.

contribution-system.s: The contribution system was the Swedish practice of extracting revenue from occupied territories, especially in Germany and the Baltic, to fund the armies stationed there. It allowed a poor and thinly populated kingdom to maintain great-power forces.

control-of-trade-routes.s: Control of trade routes refers to the dominance of key commercial corridors, chokepoints and entrepôts, allowing a state to tax, protect or monopolise the flow of goods. It was a recurring basis of imperial wealth and power, financing armies and courts without the need for…

convention-of-kanagawa.s: The Convention of Kanagawa was the treaty signed in 1854 between the Tokugawa shogunate and the United States, following Commodore Matthew Perry's expedition. It opened two ports to American vessels and ended Japan's policy of national seclusion.

copper.s: Copper is a reddish metal used since ancient times for tools, ornaments and, alloyed with tin, bronze. It was traded widely in the ancient Near East by states such as the Akkadian, Babylonian and Hittite empires.

copper-ingot.s: Copper ingots are cast bars or shapes of copper used for trade and storage of value. In Central Africa, cross-shaped copper ingots served as a form of currency and prestige good.

copper-plate-inscriptions.s: Copper plate inscriptions are legal records engraved on copper sheets, used in India to document royal land grants. In the Gupta Empire they recorded grants of land to Brahmin priests and Buddhist monasteries.

copperbelt.s: The Copperbelt is a region of rich copper deposits straddling the border of present-day Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It has been mined since early times.

copts.s: The Copts are the native Christians of Egypt, whose church traces its origins to the early Christian community of Alexandria. After the Arab conquest they remained the majority of Egypt's population for centuries.

cordoba.s: Córdoba is a city in Andalusia, southern Spain, on the Guadalquivir River. It was the capital of the Umayyad emirate and later caliphate of al-Andalus, founded by Abd al-Rahman I after the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate in the east, and one of the largest cities of medieval…

cornelis-de-houtman.s: Cornelis de Houtman was a Dutch explorer who led the first Dutch expedition to the East Indies, which sailed in 1595. Although only about a third of the crew survived, the voyage proved the route commercially viable.

coromandel-coast.s: The Coromandel Coast is the southeastern coast of the Indian subcontinent, along the Bay of Bengal. It was a major centre of textile production and trade.

coronation-of-charlemagne.s: The coronation of Charlemagne took place in Rome on Christmas Day 800 CE, when Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king as emperor. It revived the imperial title in the West for the first time since the fifth century.

coronation-of-nabopolassar.s: The coronation of Nabopolassar took place in Babylon in 626 BCE, after the Chaldean leader seized the city and declared independence from Assyria. It exploited the succession disputes following the death of Ashurbanipal.

coronation-of-shivaji.s: The coronation of Shivaji took place in 1674 at Raigad, where he was crowned as Chhatrapati with elaborate Vedic rites. It proclaimed him a sovereign Hindu king independent of the Mughals and the Deccan sultanates.

corpus-juris-civilis.s: The Corpus Juris Civilis is the body of Roman law compiled on the orders of the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, completed in 534 CE. It comprised the Code, the Digest, the Institutes and the Novels.

corruption.s: Corruption, the abuse of public office for private gain, is a recurring cause of imperial decline. It drained revenues, weakened armies and administration, and eroded the legitimacy of rulers in the eyes of their subjects.

corsica.s: Corsica is a mountainous island in the western Mediterranean, north of Sardinia. It lay within the sphere of Carthaginian influence before Rome seized it, together with Sardinia, in 238–237 BCE during the Mercenary War.

corvee-labour.s: Corvée labour is unpaid work required by a state from its subjects, often for building and maintaining public works or for military service. The Han Dynasty imposed labour obligations on its peasant population, following the punishing demands that had destroyed the Qin.

corvus.s: The corvus was a boarding bridge with a spike at its end, used by the Roman navy during the First Punic War. It allowed Roman soldiers to board and fight on Carthaginian ships as if on land.

cossacks.s: The Cossacks were self-governing communities of warriors in the steppe borderlands of Ukraine and southern Russia. In the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the uprising led by Bohdan Khmelnytsky from 1648 caused catastrophic losses.

cotton.s: Cotton is a plant fibre spun and woven into textiles, one of the most important traded commodities in history. Indian cotton textiles were exported widely under the Gupta, Mughal and Maratha empires, and cotton was cultivated in Central Asia and the Punjab.

council-of-elders-carthage.s: The Council of Elders was a governing body of Carthage, composed of members of the city's aristocracy. Together with the larger senate and the elected suffetes, it formed part of the constitution of the Punic Empire.

council-of-the-indies.s: The Council of the Indies was the supreme administrative and judicial body for Spain's American and Asian colonies, established in 1524. It drafted laws, advised the king on appointments and heard appeals.

count-palatine.s: The Count Palatine of the Rhine was one of the leading princes of the Holy Roman Empire. Under the Golden Bull of 1356, he was one of the seven electors who chose the emperor.

counterweight-trebuchet.s: A counterweight trebuchet is a siege engine that uses a heavy falling weight to swing a throwing arm, capable of hurling large stones over long distances. During the siege of Xiangyang, Persian engineers introduced counterweight trebuchets that outranged Chinese catapults.

court-of-the-one-hundred-and-four.n: Court of the One Hundred and Four
court-of-the-one-hundred-and-four.s: The Court of the One Hundred and Four was a judicial body of ancient Carthage. It held generals accountable for military failures, sometimes punishing defeated commanders severely.

cowrie-shell.s: The cowrie shell is the shell of a small sea snail, used as currency across Africa and Asia. Cowries imported from the Indian Ocean became a standard currency in West Africa.

crete.s: Crete is the largest Greek island, in the eastern Mediterranean, home of the Bronze Age Minoan civilisation. Its ancient city-states were governed by magistrates called kosmoi.

crimea.s: Crimea is a peninsula on the northern coast of the Black Sea. It was ruled by a succession of steppe powers and later by the Crimean Khanate, a vassal of the Ottoman Empire from the fifteenth century.

crimean-war.s: The Crimean War was fought from 1853 to 1856 between the Russian Empire and an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France and Sardinia. Much of the fighting centred on the siege of Sevastopol in Crimea.

criollo-people.s: Criollos, or creoles, were people of Spanish descent born in the Americas during the colonial period. They formed much of the colonial elite but were often excluded from the highest offices in favour of Spanish-born officials.

crisis-of-the-third-century.s: The Crisis of the Third Century was a period of turmoil in the Roman Empire from 235 to 284 CE. It was marked by rapid turnover of emperors, civil wars, invasions on several frontiers, plague and severe economic and monetary problems.

cristovao-da-gama.s: Cristóvão da Gama was a Portuguese commander, a son of Vasco da Gama, who led about 400 musketeers to support the Ethiopian Empire against the Adal Sultanate in 1541. He won several engagements before being captured and executed by Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi in 1542.

croats.s: The Croats are a South Slavic people whose homeland lies in present-day Croatia. Croatia was linked to the Hungarian crown and later formed part of the Habsburg lands.

croesus.s: Croesus was the last king of Lydia in western Anatolia, ruling in the sixth century BCE and proverbial for his wealth. He was defeated by Cyrus the Great at the Battle of Thymbra in 546 BCE, after which Sardis was captured.

crossbow.s: A crossbow is a bow mounted horizontally on a stock, shot by a trigger mechanism, allowing troops with limited training to shoot powerful bolts. Chinese armies used crossbows on a large scale from early times.

crossing-of-the-rubicon.s: The crossing of the Rubicon was Julius Caesar's decision in 49 BCE to lead his army across the Rubicon River in northern Italy, the boundary of his province, in defiance of the Senate. The act began a civil war that ended with Caesar's dictatorship.

crown-colony.s: A Crown Colony was a British colonial territory governed directly by the British crown, usually through an appointed governor, rather than through local self-government. The British Empire administered many of its territories in this way.

crucifixion.s: Crucifixion is a method of execution in which the condemned is fastened to a cross or stake and left to die. It was used in the ancient Mediterranean by Carthaginians, Persians and Romans.

crusade.s: A crusade was a war sanctioned by the papacy, typically against Muslims or other perceived enemies of the Church, in which participants received spiritual privileges. The crusades in the Levant brought conflict with the Seljuk Empire, the Fatimid Caliphate and the Ayyubid…

crusader-states.s: The Crusader states were Latin Christian states established in the Levant after the First Crusade, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli. They fought against the Seljuks and later the Ayyubid Empire…

crusades.s: The Crusades were a series of religious wars launched by Latin Christians from the late eleventh century, chiefly to capture and hold Jerusalem and the Holy Land. The First Crusade took advantage of the fragmentation of the Seljuk Empire after the death of Malik Shah.

ctesiphon.s: Ctesiphon was a city on the Tigris River in central Iraq, near present-day Baghdad. It was the capital of the Parthian Empire and then of the Sasanian Empire, whose great vaulted palace hall, the Taq Kasra, still partly stands.

cuauhtemoc.s: Cuauhtémoc was the last ruler of Tenochtitlan and of the Aztec Empire. He led the defence of the city during the Spanish siege and was captured in 1521 when Tenochtitlan fell.

cuba.s: Cuba is the largest island of the Caribbean, colonised by Spain from the early sixteenth century. It remained one of the last colonies of the Spanish Empire until 1898, with a plantation economy built on enslaved African labour.

cuitlahuac.s: Cuitláhuac was the ruler of Tenochtitlan who succeeded Moctezuma II in 1520. He led the Aztec forces that drove the Spanish out of the city during La Noche Triste.

cultivation-system.s: The Cultivation System was a policy introduced by the Dutch colonial government in Java from 1830, requiring villagers to devote part of their land or labour to export crops such as coffee, sugar and indigo for the state. It produced large profits for the Netherlands.

cultural-patronage.s: Cultural patronage is the sponsorship of art, architecture, literature and learning by rulers and elites. It was a recurring means by which empires displayed legitimacy, attracted talent and left lasting legacies.

cuneiform.s: Cuneiform is a writing system of wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay tablets, invented in Mesopotamia in the late fourth millennium BCE. It was used to write Sumerian, Akkadian, Elamite, Hittite and other languages for some three thousand years.

cupbearer.s: A cupbearer was a court official who served drinks to the king, a position of trust and access to the ruler. Sargon of Akkad began his career as cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish.

cura-annonae.s: The cura annonae was the Roman system for supplying grain to the city of Rome, including the free distribution of grain, the annona, to citizens. It relied on grain shipments from Egypt, North Africa and Sicily.

cursus-publicus.s: The cursus publicus was the state courier and transport service of the Roman Empire, established by Augustus, with relay stations along the main roads. It carried official messages, officials and goods.

customs-and-commercial-revenue.s: Customs and commercial revenue refers to state income from duties, tolls and taxes on trade, as opposed to land taxes. Empires that controlled ports, crossings and trade routes could draw large revenues from passing commerce, funding armies and courts.

customs-union.s: A customs union is an agreement among territories to remove tariffs between them and adopt a common external tariff. The Austro-Hungarian Empire formed a single customs union covering about fifty million people for fifty years.

cyaxares.s: Cyaxares was king of the Medes in the late seventh and early sixth centuries BCE and the main architect of the Median Empire. Allied with Nabopolassar of Babylon, he sacked Assur in 614 BCE and helped destroy Nineveh in 612 BCE.

cyprus.s: Cyprus is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean, valued for its copper. In the Late Bronze Age it corresponded with Egypt in the Amarna diplomatic letters of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom.

cyrenaica.s: Cyrenaica is the eastern coastal region of present-day Libya, named after the ancient Greek city of Cyrene. It lay on the routes between Egypt and the Maghreb.

cyril-and-methodius.s: Cyril and Methodius were Byzantine Greek brothers and missionaries of the ninth century who worked among the Slavs of central Europe. They created the Glagolitic alphabet and translated liturgical texts into Old Church Slavonic.

cyrus-cylinder.s: The Cyrus Cylinder is an inscribed clay cylinder issued after the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE. Written in Akkadian cuneiform, it presents Cyrus the Great as chosen by the god Marduk and describes the restoration of temples and deported peoples.

cyrus-the-great.s: Cyrus the Great, or Cyrus II, was the founder of the Achaemenid Empire, who acceded in 559 BCE as king of Anshan. He overthrew the Median Empire, defeated Croesus of Lydia and conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, ending the Chaldean Empire.

cyrus-the-younger.s: Cyrus the Younger was a Persian prince of the late fifth century BCE, a son of Darius II. In 401 BCE he hired Greek mercenaries in a bid to seize the throne from his brother Artaxerxes II, but was killed at the Battle of Cunaxa.

czechoslovakia.s: Czechoslovakia was a state in central Europe created in 1918 from the Czech lands of Bohemia and Moravia and from Slovakia. It was one of the successor states that emerged from the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

czechs.s: The Czechs are a West Slavic people of Bohemia and Moravia, in the present-day Czech Republic. Within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Czechs pressed for autonomy comparable to that given to Hungary in 1867, leading to persistent political conflict, especially in Bohemia.

chinese-red-army.s: The Chinese Red Army was the armed force of the Chinese Communist Party, formed from units that rebelled against the Nationalists in 1927 and 1928. Led by Zhu De and Mao Zedong, it defended the Chinese Soviet Republic in Jiangxi until the Long March of 1934–1935.

central-provinces.s: The Central Provinces was a province of British India formed in 1861 from the Nagpur and Saugor and Nerbudda territories, with its capital at Nagpur. Berar was joined to it in 1903, and from 1936 it was called the Central Provinces and Berar.

charles-ii-of-england.s: Charles II of England was king of England, Scotland and Ireland, restored to the throne in 1660 after the Commonwealth. His marriage to Catherine of Braganza brought Tangier and Bombay to England, and he granted charters for Carolina, Pennsylvania and the Hudson's Bay Company…

charles-ii-of-spain.s: Charles II of Spain was the last Habsburg king of Spain, reigning from 1665 to 1700. Sickly and childless, he presided over a period of economic weakness and military losses to France.

charles-ii-archduke-of-austria.s: Charles II, Archduke of Austria, was a younger son of Emperor Ferdinand I who received Inner Austria, ruling Styria, Carinthia and Carniola from Graz from 1564. He organised defences against Ottoman raids along the Croatian frontier and invited the Jesuits to Graz to promote…

charles-ii-margrave-of-baden-durlach.s: Charles II, Margrave of Baden-Durlach, ruled the margraviate from 1553 to 1577. He introduced the Lutheran Reformation in 1556 after the Peace of Augsburg allowed princes to choose their territory's faith, and in 1565 moved his residence from Pforzheim to Durlach, giving the…

charles-ii-count-of-hohenzollern-sigmari.s: Charles II, Count of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, was a son of Count Charles I of Hohenzollern. When his father's lands were divided in 1576 he received Sigmaringen and Veringen on the upper Danube, founding the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line.

charles-ii-grand-duke-of-mecklenburg-str.n: Charles II, Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz
charles-ii-grand-duke-of-mecklenburg-str.s: Charles II, Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, ruled the duchy from 1794 and was raised to grand duke by the Congress of Vienna in 1815. He was a brother of Queen Charlotte, wife of George III, and father of Queen Louise of Prussia.

charles-ii-duke-of-brunswick.s: Charles II, Duke of Brunswick, succeeded his father, who was killed at Quatre Bras in 1815, and took power in 1823. His arbitrary rule provoked a rising in September 1830 that burned his palace and drove him out.

carthago-nova.s: Carthago Nova, modern Cartagena in south-east Spain, was founded around 227 BCE by the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal the Fair as the capital of Barcid Iberia, with a fine harbour and nearby silver mines. Scipio Africanus captured it in 209 BCE.

charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden.n: Charles Frederick, Grand Duke of Baden
charles-frederick-grand-duke-of-baden.s: Charles Frederick of Baden ruled for 73 years, first as Margrave of Baden-Durlach from 1738. In 1771 he inherited Baden-Baden and reunited the margraviate.

charles-frederick-duke-of-holstein-gotto.s: Charles Frederick, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp, lost the ducal part of Schleswig to Denmark in the Great Northern War, a loss confirmed in 1720. He found support in Russia and married Anna Petrovna, daughter of Peter the Great.

charles-the-bald.s: Charles the Bald was the youngest son of Louis the Pious. By the Treaty of Verdun in 843 he received West Francia, the forerunner of France, and in 875 he was crowned emperor.

chota-nagpur-plateau.s: The Chota Nagpur Plateau is an upland of forests and minerals in eastern India, covering most of modern Jharkhand and parts of Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal. It is home to Adivasi peoples such as the Munda and Oraon.

constantine-vii.s: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus was Byzantine emperor, nominally from 913 and in real power from 945 to 959. A scholar-emperor, he sponsored the treatise known as De Administrando Imperio, written for his son, which describes the peoples around the empire, including the Serbs,…

charles-iii-of-spain.s: Charles III of Spain, previously king of Naples and Sicily, ruled Spain from 1759 to 1788. An enlightened reformer, he promoted roads, trade, academies and royal factories and expelled the Jesuits in 1767.

charles-iii-prince-of-monaco.s: Charles III, Prince of Monaco, ruled from 1856 to 1889. After Menton and Roquebrune broke away in 1848, he sold Monaco's claims to them to France in 1861, leaving only the small principality.

charles-iii-duke-of-bourbon.s: Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, was Constable of France and the greatest noble of the kingdom. When Francis I and his mother challenged his inheritance, he went over to Emperor Charles V in 1523, and his lands were confiscated.

communist-party-of-the-soviet-union.n: Communist Party of the Soviet Union
communist-party-of-the-soviet-union.s: The Communist Party of the Soviet Union grew out of Lenin's Bolshevik faction and took power in the October Revolution of 1917. It was the only legal party of the Soviet Union, governing through soviets and the secret police, with branches led by first secretaries in each…

cesare-borgia.s: Cesare Borgia was the son of Pope Alexander VI. Made Duke of Valentinois by Louis XII of France in 1498, he used papal money and French troops to conquer the lordships of the Romagna and the Marche, including Imola, Forlì, Rimini, Pesaro, Faenza and Camerino, forming a Duchy…

cape-coast.s: Cape Coast is a port town on the coast of present-day Ghana, in the lands of the Akan kingdom of Fetu. The Swedish Africa Company built Fort Carolusborg there in 1653, which passed through Danish and Dutch hands before the English took it in 1664 and made Cape Coast Castle…

central-america.s: Central America is the narrow land bridge between Mexico and South America, today divided among Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. Its Pacific lowlands received Nahua-speaking migrants from central Mexico, and from the 16th century most…

chen-sheng.s: Chen Sheng was a conscript leader who began the first great rising against the Qin dynasty in 209 BCE. Delayed by rain and facing execution, he and Wu Guang rebelled at Dazexiang, took the city of Chen and proclaimed the state of Zhangchu, reviving the name of Chu.

chiang-kai-shek.s: Chiang Kai-shek was a Chinese military and political leader who headed the Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang, after Sun Yat-sen. Commander of the Northern Expedition, he established the Nationalist Government at Nanjing in 1928, fought the Communists and regional rivals, and…

conrad-ii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Conrad II was the first Salian king of Germany, elected in 1024 and crowned emperor in Rome in 1027. He put down the revolt of his stepson Duke Ernest II of Swabia, granted counties in the Alpine valleys to the bishops of Trent and Brixen to secure the routes to Italy, and in…

cantabrian-wars.s: The Cantabrian Wars were Rome's final conquest of the Iberian Peninsula, fought from 29 to 19 BCE against the Cantabri and Astures of the northern mountains. Augustus took personal command in 26–25 BCE, and his general Agrippa completed the subjugation in 19 BCE after fierce…

cecil-rhodes.s: Cecil Rhodes was a British businessman and politician in southern Africa who made a fortune in Kimberley diamonds through De Beers and in gold. Prime Minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896, he used his British South Africa Company to occupy Mashonaland in 1890 and…

chao-phraya-river.s: The Chao Phraya is the main river of central Thailand, formed at Nakhon Sawan by the meeting of the Ping and the Nan and flowing south past Ayutthaya and Bangkok into the Gulf of Thailand. Its fertile flood plain supported the Dvaravati towns, Lavo and Suphannaphum, and the…

clemens-august-of-bavaria.s: Clemens August of Bavaria was a Wittelsbach prince who gathered church offices on a grand scale, becoming Archbishop-Elector of Cologne from 1723, Prince-Bishop of Münster, Paderborn, Hildesheim and Osnabrück, and Grand Master of the Teutonic Order. He thus ruled a large part…

cold-war.s: The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies from the late 1940s to 1991. It divided Europe, including Germany, into opposing blocs and was fought through an arms race, propaganda and proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam,…

charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor.s: Charles VI was Holy Roman Emperor from 1711 to 1740 and the last male Habsburg of the senior line. A claimant to Spain in the War of the Spanish Succession, he received instead the Spanish Netherlands, Milan and Naples in 1713–1714, and won the Banat from the Ottomans in 1718.

charles-vi-of-france.s: Charles VI, called the Beloved and later the Mad, was King of France from 1380 to 1422. His recurring bouts of insanity from 1392 left power to rival princes and led to civil war between the Armagnac and Burgundian factions.

cao-bang.s: Cao Bằng is a mountainous province of northern Vietnam on the border with China. After the Lê restoration took Thăng Long in 1592, members of the Mạc dynasty fled there and, with Ming protection, held a rump state until 1677.

cape-dutch.s: Cape Dutch was the form of Dutch spoken at the Cape of Good Hope by settlers, the enslaved and Khoekhoe communities from the 17th century. Simplified and influenced by Malay, Portuguese and Khoekhoe, it gradually developed into Afrikaans.

cape-town.s: Cape Town is a port city on Table Bay in south-western South Africa. It was founded in 1652 by Jan van Riebeeck as a supply station of the Dutch East India Company and grew into the capital of the Cape Colony, under Dutch and then British rule.

central-plain-china.s: The Central Plain, Zhongyuan in Chinese, is the region of the middle and lower Yellow River, roughly modern Henan and neighbouring areas. It was the heartland of the Shang and Zhou states and was seen as the centre of Chinese civilisation.

chao-phra-fang.s: Chao Phra Fang was a militant Buddhist monk from Fang who set up a regime at Sawangkhaburi in northern Siam after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767. He seized the Phitsanulok regime's territory in 1768.

charles-vii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Charles VII, born Charles Albert, was Elector of Bavaria from 1726. On the death of Charles VI he refused to accept Maria Theresa's succession and, with French support, was elected Holy Roman Emperor in 1742, the first non-Habsburg in three centuries.

charles-albert-of-sardinia.s: Charles Albert was King of Sardinia from 1831. In 1848 he granted the Statuto Albertino, a constitution that later became Italy's, and declared war on Austria in support of the Lombard revolt.

charles-i-of-anjou.s: Charles I of Anjou was the youngest brother of Louis IX of France, Count of Anjou and of Provence through his marriage to Beatrice of Provence in 1246. Invited by the pope, he defeated the Hohenstaufen and took the Kingdom of Sicily in 1266.

charles-the-bold.s: Charles the Bold was Duke of Burgundy from 1467, ruling the Burgundian lands of France and the Low Countries. He sacked rebellious Liège in 1468, bought Guelders in 1473 and sought a royal crown to link his territories.

chen-yu.s: Chen Yu was a general of the revived state of Zhao during the rebellion against the Qin dynasty and a sworn friend, later bitter enemy, of Zhang Er. Passed over by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, he drove Zhang Er from Changshan, restored Zhao Xie and took the Kingdom of Dai.

connecticut-river.s: The Connecticut River is the longest river in New England, flowing south from near the Canadian border to Long Island Sound. English settlers founded Hartford, Windsor and Wethersfield on its banks in the 1630s, and Saybrook guarded its mouth.

crimean-tatars.s: The Crimean Tatars are a Turkic Muslim people of the Crimean peninsula. They formed the core of the Crimean Khanate, an Ottoman vassal, until Russia annexed Crimea in 1783, after which many emigrated to Ottoman lands.

crown-dependencies.s: The Crown Dependencies are the Bailiwick of Jersey, the Bailiwick of Guernsey and the Isle of Man, self-governing possessions of the British Crown. They are not part of the United Kingdom, have their own parliaments and laws, and rely on the UK for defence and foreign relations.

commentarii-de-bello-gallico.s: Commentarii de Bello Gallico is Julius Caesar's account of his wars in Gaul from 58 to 52 BCE, written in the third person. Besides the campaigns, it describes the peoples of Gaul, Germany and Britain, including his two expeditions to Britain in 55 and 54 BCE.

chanda-sahib.s: Chanda Sahib was a commander of the Nawab of the Carnatic who seized Madurai and Tiruchirappalli in the 1730s. Captured by the Marathas in 1741, he was released and with French backing became Nawab of the Carnatic in 1749.

charles-alexander-margrave-of-brandenbur.s: Charles Alexander was the last Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach, from 1757, who also inherited Brandenburg-Bayreuth in 1769. Like his predecessors he hired out soldiers to Britain during the American war.

charles-alexander-grand-duke-of-saxe-wei.n: Charles Alexander, Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach
charles-alexander-grand-duke-of-saxe-wei.s: Charles Alexander was Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach from 1853 until his death in 1901. He continued Weimar's cultural tradition, supporting Franz Liszt, founding an art school and restoring the Wartburg castle.

charleston-south-carolina.s: Charleston, founded in 1670 as Charles Town, is a port city in South Carolina. It was the capital and main port of the Carolina colony, shipping rice and indigo grown by enslaved Africans, and one of the largest towns in colonial British North America.

chaubise-rajya.s: The Chaubise Rajya, the 'twenty-four kingdoms', were a group of small hill principalities in the Gandaki region of western Nepal, many ruled by dynasties claiming Rajput descent. Palpa, Tanahun and Lamjung were among the strongest.

chen-gongbo.s: Chen Gongbo was a founding member of the Chinese Communist Party who later joined the Kuomintang and followed Wang Jingwei into collaboration with Japan. He served as a leading official of the Japanese-backed Nanjing government and became its acting head after Wang's death in…

chitpavan-brahmins.s: The Chitpavan Brahmins are a Brahmin community from the Konkan coast of western India. Their influence grew in the 18th century, when the Peshwas, the hereditary chief ministers of the Maratha state, came from the community.

christian-iv-of-denmark.s: Christian IV was King of Denmark and Norway from 1588 to 1648. He founded towns such as Glückstadt and Christiania and built palaces including Rosenborg in Copenhagen.

classic-maya-collapse.s: The Classic Maya collapse was the decline and abandonment of the lowland Maya kingdoms of Guatemala, Belize and southern Mexico between the 8th and 10th centuries. Royal dynasties stopped erecting dated monuments and great cities were deserted.

claude-maxwell-macdonald.s: Sir Claude MacDonald was a British soldier and diplomat who became commissioner and consul-general of the Oil Rivers Protectorate in 1891, setting up an administration at Old Calabar. The territory became the Niger Coast Protectorate in 1893.
