clemens-wenceslaus-of-saxony.s: Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony was a son of the Elector of Saxony who became Prince-Bishop of Augsburg in 1768 and in the same year the last Archbishop-Elector of Trier. He fled the French revolutionary armies in 1794, and in 1803 his electorate was dissolved.

cleomenes-iii.s: Cleomenes III was King of Sparta from about 235 BCE. He cancelled debts, redistributed land and enlarged the citizen body, then fought the Achaean League in the Cleomenean War, taking cities such as Tegea.

code-noir.s: The Code Noir was a decree issued by Louis XIV in 1685 to regulate slavery in the French colonies of the Caribbean. It defined enslaved people as property, set harsh punishments, required Catholic baptism and restricted freedom for the enslaved.

codrus.s: Codrus was a legendary last King of Athens who was said to have sacrificed himself to save the city from a Dorian invasion. Greek tradition held that his sons led the Ionian migration across the Aegean, Neleus founding Miletus and Androclus Ephesus, so many Ionian cities…

colonial-office.s: The Colonial Office was the British government department that administered most of Britain's colonies, separated from the War Office in 1854. Crown colonies and protectorates were governed by officials who reported to the Secretary of State for the Colonies.

congal-caech.s: Congal Cáech was king of the Dál nAraidi and of Ulaid in north-eastern Ireland, and is said to have claimed the high kingship of Tara. Allied with Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata, he fought the Uí Néill high king Domnall mac Áedo and was killed at the Battle of Mag Rath in 637.

congress-of-berlin.s: The Congress of Berlin was a meeting of the great powers chaired by Bismarck in June and July 1878 to revise the Treaty of San Stefano after the Russo-Turkish War. It recognised the independence of Serbia, Montenegro and Romania, divided Bulgaria, creating Eastern Rumelia, and…

conrad-of-montferrat.s: Conrad of Montferrat was an Italian nobleman who arrived at Tyre in 1187 and held it against Saladin after the fall of Jerusalem. He became Marquis of Montferrat and, through marriage to Isabella, claimant to the crown of Jerusalem, and was elected king in April 1192.

council-of-regency-of-spain-and-the-indi.n: Council of Regency of Spain and the Indies
council-of-regency-of-spain-and-the-indi.s: The Council of Regency of Spain and the Indies governed Spain in the name of the captive Ferdinand VII during the Peninsular War, replacing the Supreme Central Junta in 1810. Based at Cádiz, it summoned the Cortes that wrote the constitution of 1812.

caesarea-philippi.s: Caesarea Philippi was an ancient city at the springs of the Jordan below Mount Hermon, on the site of the shrine of Pan at Paneas. Herod's son Philip the Tetrarch rebuilt it around 2 BCE and made it his capital, naming it after Augustus.

camilo-torres-tenorio.s: Camilo Torres Tenorio was a lawyer from Popayán and a leading figure of New Granada's independence movement. His Memorial de Agravios of 1809 protested against Spain's unequal treatment of the American colonies.

camino-real-de-tierra-adentro.s: The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro was the Spanish colonial royal road running some 2,500 km north from Mexico City through the silver-mining towns of New Spain to Santa Fe in New Mexico. Juan de Oñate's colonists travelled it in 1598, and supply caravans, missionaries,…

cantonal-rebellion.s: The Cantonal Rebellion was an uprising of intransigent federal republicans in southern and eastern Spain during the First Spanish Republic. From July 1873 cities such as Cartagena, Cádiz, Seville and Granada proclaimed themselves sovereign cantons.

cape-lopez.s: Cape Lopez is a headland at the mouth of the Ogooué delta on the coast of Gabon, near modern Port-Gentil, named after the 15th-century Portuguese navigator Lopo Gonçalves. Its sheltered bay made it a trading point for European ships.

carlos-duke-of-madrid.s: Carlos, Duke of Madrid, was the Carlist claimant to the Spanish throne as Carlos VII from 1868. He led the Third Carlist War of 1872–1876, setting up a court and administration at Estella in Navarre that governed much of the Basque Country and Navarre.

carnatic-wars.s: The Carnatic Wars were three conflicts in south-eastern India in which the British and French East India Companies backed rival claimants to the Carnatic and Hyderabad. Robert Clive's defence of Arcot in 1751 and the British victory at Wandiwash in 1760 broke French power.

casimir-ii-the-just.s: Casimir II the Just was a Piast duke, the youngest son of Bolesław III Wrymouth. He inherited the Duchy of Sandomierz in 1166 and seized Kraków and the senior throne from his brother Mieszko III in 1177.

casimir-iii-the-great.s: Casimir III the Great was King of Poland from 1333 to 1370, the last of the Piast kings. He made peace with Bohemia and the Teutonic Knights, annexed Red Ruthenia, codified the laws of the kingdom and founded the University of Kraków in 1364.

casimir-iv-jagiellon.s: Casimir IV Jagiellon was Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1440 and King of Poland from 1447. He backed the Prussian Confederation against the Teutonic Order, and the Thirteen Years' War ended with the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466, which gave Poland Royal Prussia.

cassius-dio.s: Cassius Dio was a Greek-speaking Roman senator and historian from Nicaea in Bithynia. His Roman History in 80 books covered Rome from its founding to 229 CE, and survives partly in later summaries.

castruccio-castracani.s: Castruccio Castracani was a Ghibelline condottiero who became lord of Lucca in 1316. He defeated Florence at Altopascio in 1325, took Pistoia and built a large Tuscan state, and Emperor Louis IV made him Duke of Lucca in 1327.

central-india-agency.s: The Central India Agency was the British political agency that supervised the princely states of central India, including Indore, Gwalior, Bhopal and many small Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand states. An Agent to the Governor-General based at Indore oversaw subordinate agencies.

central-rada.s: The Central Rada was the Ukrainian revolutionary council formed in Kyiv in March 1917 under the historian Mykhailo Hrushevsky. Through its Universals it proclaimed Ukrainian autonomy, then the Ukrainian People's Republic, and full independence in January 1918.

centurione-ii-zaccaria.s: Centurione II Zaccaria was the last Prince of Achaea, a member of a Genoese family that held the barony of Arcadia in the Peloponnese. He seized the principality in 1404.

chach-nama.s: The Chach Nama is a Persian chronicle of the Arab conquest of Sindh, translated by Ali Kufi around 1226 from what it claims was an earlier Arabic work. It tells of the Rai dynasty, the rise of the Brahmin chamberlain Chach and the fall of his son Dahir to Muhammad ibn Qasim in…

chan-chan.s: Chan Chan was the capital of the Chimú kingdom on the north coast of Peru, near modern Trujillo, and the largest adobe city of the pre-Columbian Americas. It contained some ten walled royal compounds with courts, storerooms and burial platforms decorated with relief friezes.

changchub-gyaltsen.s: Changchub Gyaltsen was the myriarch of Phagmodru who overthrew the Mongol-backed Sakya regime in central Tibet in the 1350s. Founder of the Phagmodrupa dynasty, he revived Tibetan traditions of the old empire, reorganised the country into districts under fortress governors and…

char-bouba-war.s: The Char Bouba war was a conflict in south-western Mauritania between the Berber Zawaya scholarly tribes, led by the reforming imam Nasir al-Din, and Hassani Arab warrior groups. The Hassani won by about 1677.

charles-augustus-grand-duke-of-saxe-weim.n: Charles Augustus, Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach
charles-augustus-grand-duke-of-saxe-weim.s: Charles Augustus, Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, ruled the duchy from 1775, first under his mother Anna Amalia's guidance. He brought Goethe to Weimar as friend and minister, and Herder and Schiller followed, making the small court the centre of German classicism.

charles-edward-duke-of-saxe-coburg-and-g.n: Charles Edward, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
charles-edward-duke-of-saxe-coburg-and-g.s: Charles Edward, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, was a grandson of Queen Victoria, born Duke of Albany in Britain, who inherited the German duchy in 1900. He fought for Germany in the First World War, was stripped of his British titles and abdicated in November 1918.

charles-george-gordon.s: Charles George Gordon was a British army officer who commanded the Ever Victorious Army against the Taiping in China. As governor-general of the Sudan for the Khedivate of Egypt from 1877 to 1879 he campaigned against the slave trade.

charles-i-of-hungary.s: Charles I of Hungary, also called Charles Robert, was the first Angevin king of Hungary, who won the throne after the Árpád line died out in 1301. By 1321 he had broken the power of great oligarchs such as Matthew Csák.

charles-i-count-palatine-of-birkenfeld.n: Charles I, Count Palatine of Birkenfeld
charles-i-count-palatine-of-birkenfeld.s: Charles I, Count Palatine of Birkenfeld, was a younger son of Duke Wolfgang of Palatinate-Zweibrücken, who received Birkenfeld in the Hunsrück in the 1569 division of his father's lands. He founded the Birkenfeld branch of the House of Wittelsbach, whose descendants later…

charles-ii-duke-of-parma.s: Charles II, Duke of Parma, born Charles Louis of Bourbon-Parma, became King of Etruria as a small child in 1803 under his mother Maria Luisa's regency, until Napoleon ended the kingdom in 1807. He later ruled the Duchy of Lucca from 1824 to 1847 and then briefly Parma, an…

charles-ii-duke-of-guelders.s: Charles II, Duke of Guelders, known as Charles of Egmond, recovered the duchy his family had lost to Charles the Bold and fought the Habsburgs for over four decades with French support. He extended his power over Groningen, Friesland and Utrecht.

charles-iv-duke-of-anjou.s: Charles IV, Duke of Anjou, also called Charles of Maine, was the nephew and heir of René of Anjou, whom he succeeded as Count of Provence in 1480. Childless, he bequeathed Provence, Maine and the Angevin claims to Naples to King Louis XI on his death in 1481.

chauhan.s: The Chauhans are a Rajput clan of northern and western India, descended in tradition from the Chahamana dynasties that ruled Shakambhari and Ajmer, whose best-known king, Prithviraj Chauhan, fell to Muhammad of Ghor in 1192. Branches of the clan later ruled many smaller states…

cheddi-jagan.s: Cheddi Jagan was a Guyanese politician of Indian descent who founded the People's Progressive Party. He won the 1953 elections in British Guiana, but Britain suspended the constitution after 133 days, fearing his Marxist views.

chen-li-han-dynasty.s: Chen Li was a Western Han official who served as governor of Zangke commandery in the south-west. Around 27 BCE, when Xing, the king of Yelang, resisted Han authority, Chen Li executed him and crushed the resistance of his allies.

chen-li-chen-han.s: Chen Li was the son and heir of Chen Youliang, the rebel who founded the Chen Han state in central China. After his father was killed by Zhu Yuanzhang's forces at the Battle of Lake Poyang in 1363, Chen Li succeeded him but surrendered Wuchang in 1364.

chen-shubao.s: Chen Shubao was the last emperor of the Chen dynasty, reigning from 582 to 589. Later historians portrayed him as devoted to poetry, banquets and palace favourites while neglecting defence.

chhattisgarh-feudatory-states.s: The Chhattisgarh Feudatory States were a group of fourteen small princely states in the upper Mahanadi region of central India, including Kanker, Kawardha, Sakti and Sarangarh. Formerly tributary to the Bhonsles of Nagpur, they came under British paramountcy, attached first to…

chithira-thirunal-balarama-varma.s: Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma was the last ruling Maharaja of Travancore, from 1924. His Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 opened state temples to all Hindus regardless of caste, and he founded the University of Travancore.

chlothar-ii.s: Chlothar II was a Merovingian king, son of Chilperic I and Fredegund, who became King of Neustria as an infant in 584. In 613 he defeated and executed Queen Brunhild and reunited the whole Frankish realm.

christian-i-of-denmark.s: Christian I of Denmark was the first king of the House of Oldenburg, elected in Denmark in 1448 and later king of Norway and, briefly, Sweden. In 1460 the estates of Schleswig and Holstein elected him their ruler under the Treaty of Ribe, promising the lands would stay forever…

christian-i-prince-of-anhalt-bernburg.s: Christian I, Prince of Anhalt-Bernburg, received Bernburg in the 1603 division of Anhalt. A Calvinist statesman in the service of the Palatinate, he was a chief organiser of the Protestant Union and the leading adviser of Frederick V in the Bohemian revolt.

christian-i-duke-of-saxe-merseburg.s: Christian I, Duke of Saxe-Merseburg, was a younger son of Elector John George I of Saxony. Under his father's will he received Merseburg and its secularised bishopric in 1656 and founded the secondary duchy of Saxe-Merseburg, which remained subordinate to the Saxon electorate.

christopher-codrington-1640-1698.s: Christopher Codrington was a Barbados-born planter and colonial governor who began large-scale sugar planting on Antigua in 1674. As governor-general of the Leeward Islands from 1689 he led English forces against the French during the Nine Years' War, retaking St Kitts.

church-of-england.s: The Church of England is the established Christian church of England, which broke from papal authority under Henry VIII in 1534 and took a Protestant form under Edward VI and Elizabeth I, with the monarch as supreme governor. It was established by law in several English…

cnut-the-great.s: Cnut the Great was a Danish prince, son of Sweyn Forkbeard, who conquered England in 1016 and became king of Denmark in 1018 and of Norway in 1028. Ruling this North Sea empire largely from England, he kept English law and institutions, used Danish and English earls and…

co-loa-citadel.s: Cổ Loa Citadel is an ancient fortified settlement north of Hanoi in the Red River delta, with three concentric rings of earthen ramparts and moats. Tradition credits it to King An Dương of Âu Lạc in the 3rd century BCE, and excavations have found large bronze arrowhead hoards.

conrad-i-of-burgundy.s: Conrad I of Burgundy, called the Peaceful, was king of the united Kingdom of Burgundy, or Arles, from 937 to 993. He was raised at the court of Otto I, who protected his throne, and his sister Adelaide married Otto.

constantine-ii-of-georgia.s: Constantine II of Georgia was a Bagrationi king who claimed rule over all Georgia from 1478, as the united kingdom broke apart. He fought the breakaway rulers of Imereti and Kakheti and the atabegs of Samtskhe but could not restore unity.

constantine-ii-of-greece.s: Constantine II of Greece was the last king of Greece, reigning from 1964. He clashed with the government of Georgios Papandreou and accepted the colonels' coup of April 1967, but his failed counter-coup that December forced him into exile.

constantine-iii-western-roman-emperor.s: Constantine III was a common soldier proclaimed emperor by the Roman army in Britain in 407. He took troops to Gaul to face the barbarian invaders and won control of Gaul and Hispania, and Honorius briefly recognised him.

constantine-iii-of-abkhazia.s: Constantine III of Abkhazia was king of Abkhazia from about 898 to 916. He extended the kingdom eastward into Kartli, which he annexed around 904, and campaigned against the Armenian Bagratids and the Kakhetians.

continental-system.s: The Continental System was Napoleon's embargo on British trade, decreed in Berlin in 1806 and Milan in 1807, which forbade France, its allies and dependent states from trading with Britain. It aimed to ruin the British economy but caused shortages and widespread smuggling,…

corcu-duibne.s: The Corcu Duibne were an early medieval Irish population group of west Munster, settled on the Dingle and Iveragh peninsulas of modern County Kerry. Counted among the Érainn, they were later subject to the Eóganacht kings of Iarmumu.

cottian-alps.s: The Cottian Alps are a range of the western Alps on the modern French–Italian border, crossed by the Mont Genèvre and Mont Cenis passes. They take their name from Cottius, a local king who allied with Augustus and kept his realm as a client kingdom based at Susa.

council-of-constance.s: The Council of Constance was a general council of the Catholic Church held in the imperial city of Constance, convened at the urging of King Sigismund. It ended the Western Schism by deposing or accepting the resignations of three rival popes and electing Martin V in 1417.

cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-aghtamar.n: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar
cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-aghtamar.s: The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Aghtamar island in Lake Van was built between 915 and 921 by the architect Manuel for King Gagik I Artsruni of Vaspurakan. Its outer walls are covered with relief carvings of biblical scenes, the king and animals, making it a masterpiece of…

castries.s: Castries is the capital and main port of Saint Lucia. Originally called Le Carénage for its sheltered harbour, it was renamed in 1785 after the French naval minister, the Marquis de Castries.

chhatrasal.s: Chhatrasal was a Bundela Rajput leader who fought the Mughal Empire and founded an independent kingdom in Bundelkhand, with its capital at Panna. In 1729 he called on the Maratha Peshwa Baji Rao I to help repel a Mughal attack, granting him a third of his lands.

county-of-pallars-jussa.s: The County of Pallars Jussà was the lower, southern half of the Pyrenean county of Pallars, centred on Tremp, created when Count Sunyer divided his lands in 1011. A frontier county facing the Taifa of Lérida, it expanded south by conquest and passed to the counts of Barcelona…

county-of-pallars-sobira.s: The County of Pallars Sobirà was the upper, northern half of the Pyrenean county of Pallars, centred on Sort and the Àneu valleys, created in the division of 1011. Its counts became vassals of Barcelona and Aragon but kept wide local powers, and it was the last Catalan county…

classic-of-poetry.s: The Classic of Poetry, or Shijing, is the oldest Chinese collection of poems, with 305 songs dating from the Western Zhou to the middle of the Spring and Autumn period. It includes folk songs from the states, court hymns and sacrificial odes.

cafer-seydahmet.s: Cafer Seydahmet was a Crimean Tatar politician and writer. After the Russian Revolution he served with Noman Çelebicihan in the directorate of the Crimean People's Republic of 1917 to 1918, responsible for foreign and military affairs.

cai-shu-du.s: Cai Shu Du was a son of King Wen of Zhou and brother of King Wu, who gave him the fief of Cai in Henan. After King Wu's death he joined the rebellion of the Three Guards against the regency of the Duke of Zhou.

cai-tingkai.s: Cai Tingkai was a Chinese general who commanded the 19th Route Army in its defence of Shanghai against Japan in 1932. Sent to Fujian to fight the Communists, he and other dissidents broke with Chiang Kai-shek and proclaimed the Fujian People's Government in November 1933,…

cakraningrat-iv.s: Cakraningrat IV was a prince of western Madura who ruled from the 1720s. Seeking independence from Mataram, he took part in the wars of the 1740s, first siding with the Dutch East India Company and then turning against it when it refused him eastern Java.

callias-of-chalcis.s: Callias of Chalcis was a Euboean politician who in the 340s BCE sought to unite Euboea under the leadership of Chalcis, reviving the Euboean League. He moved between alliances with Philip II of Macedon and Athens, and with Athenian help drove out pro-Macedonian tyrants on the…

canh-thinh.s: Cảnh Thịnh, born Nguyễn Quang Toản, was the second emperor of the Tây Sơn dynasty of Vietnam, succeeding his father Quang Trung as a boy in 1792. His court was weakened by factional purges and quarrels with his uncle's southern realm.

canute-lavard.s: Canute Lavard was a Danish prince, son of King Eric I, who became Duke of Schleswig around 1115. He defended the border against the Wends and gained authority among the Obotrites as their prince.

caodaism.s: Caodaism is a syncretic religion founded in southern Vietnam in 1926, with its Holy See at Tây Ninh. It combines elements of Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism and Christianity, and honours figures such as Victor Hugo as saints.

cao-huan.s: Cao Huan was the last emperor of Cao Wei, reigning from 260 to 266 as a figurehead under the Sima family. During his reign Wei conquered Shu Han in 263.

caonabo.s: Caonabo was a Taíno cacique of Maguana in central Hispaniola and husband of Anacaona of Jaragua. He is credited with destroying La Navidad, the fort left by Columbus in 1493, and killing its garrison.

cape-guardafui.s: Cape Guardafui is the headland at the tip of the Horn of Africa in north-eastern Somalia, where the Gulf of Aden meets the Indian Ocean. Its dangerous waters wrecked many ships, and the rulers of the Majeerteen Sultanate drew revenue from salvaging them, leading to agreements…

cape-horn.s: Cape Horn is the southernmost headland of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago in Chile, rounded by Dutch navigators in 1616. The sea route around it became the main passage between the Atlantic and Pacific for sailing ships until the Panama Canal opened in 1914.

carl-rover.s: Carl Röver was a German Nazi politician, Gauleiter of Weser-Ems from 1928. After the Nazis won an absolute majority in the Oldenburg state election of 1932, he became minister-president of the Free State of Oldenburg, one of the first Nazi-led state governments in Germany.

carl-ulrich.s: Carl Ulrich was a German Social Democratic politician from Offenbach. After the revolution of 1918 he became the first President of the People's State of Hesse, governing from Darmstadt until 1928 at the head of Weimar coalition governments.

carlo-armellini.s: Carlo Armellini was an Italian lawyer and politician. After Pope Pius IX fled Rome, he served in the provisional government, and in March 1849 he formed the governing triumvirate of the Roman Republic with Giuseppe Mazzini and Aurelio Saffi.

carlo-cattaneo.s: Carlo Cattaneo was an Italian philosopher, economist and federalist. During the Five Days of Milan in March 1848 he led the council of war that directed the uprising against the Austrian garrison.

carlo-i-tocco.s: Carlo I Tocco was Count palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos from about 1376 and Duke of Leucadia. He took Ioannina in 1411 and Arta in 1416, reuniting the Despotate of Epirus under his rule, and received the title of despot from the Byzantine emperor.

carlo-ii-manfredi.s: Carlo II Manfredi was lord of Faenza in Romagna from 1468 until 1477, when his brother Galeotto drove him out. He began the rebuilding of Faenza in Renaissance style, including the new cathedral designed by Giuliano da Maiano and the reshaping of the town centre around its…

carlo-lauberg.s: Carlo Lauberg was a Neapolitan chemist and Jacobin who fled to France after a republican conspiracy in 1794. He returned with the French army in January 1799 and became the first president of the provisional government of the Parthenopean Republic.

carlos-camacho.s: Carlos Camacho was a Chamorro dentist and politician from Guam. Appointed governor by President Richard Nixon in 1969, he won the territory's first gubernatorial election in 1970 and served until 1975, the first elected governor of Guam, an unincorporated territory of the…

carlos-davila.s: Carlos Dávila was a Chilean journalist, diplomat and politician. He helped overthrow President Juan Esteban Montero in June 1932, joining the junta of the Socialist Republic of Chile, then pushed out Marmaduke Grove and ruled as provisional president for about three months.

carlos-manuel-de-cespedes.s: Carlos Manuel de Céspedes was a Cuban planter and lawyer who freed his enslaved workers and proclaimed Cuban independence at his estate of La Demajagua on 10 October 1868, starting the Ten Years' War against Spain. In 1869 the assembly of Guáimaro elected him first President…

carlos-montufar.s: Carlos Montúfar was a Quito aristocrat and soldier, son of the Marquis of Selva Alegre. Sent to Quito in 1810 as a royal commissioner of the Regency, he sided with the patriots and promoted the second junta.

carol-i-of-romania.s: Carol I, a German prince of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, was elected Prince of the United Principalities of Romania in 1866. He led Romania in the war of 1877 to 1878 against the Ottomans, which won full independence, and was crowned the first King of Romania in 1881.

caroline-islands.s: The Caroline Islands are a widely scattered archipelago in the western Pacific north of New Guinea, including Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae and Palau. Their peoples built chiefdoms with monumental centres such as Nan Madol and Leluh.

carta-de-logu.s: The Carta de Logu is a law code issued in the Sardinian language by Eleanor of Arborea in 1392, revising an earlier code of her father Marianus IV. It covered civil and criminal law, rural life and the rights of women.

casimir-i-of-kuyavia.s: Casimir I of Kuyavia was a Piast duke, son of Konrad I of Masovia, who received Kuyavia in 1233 and Łęczyca after his father's death in 1247. He fought his neighbours and the Teutonic Order over Pomerania and border lands.

caspian-flotilla.s: The Caspian Flotilla is the Russian naval force on the Caspian Sea, founded under Peter the Great in 1722. In 1918 its sailors at Baku helped bring down the Baku Commune, and the Centrocaspian committee of the flotilla gave its name to the government that replaced it.

caste-war-of-yucatan.s: The Caste War of Yucatán was a long uprising of the Maya against the Hispanic and mestizo elites of the Yucatán Peninsula. Beginning at Tepich in 1847, it nearly drove the whites to Mérida and Campeche, forcing Yucatán to rejoin Mexico in 1848.

castel-di-castro.s: Castel di Castro is the fortified hilltop quarter of Cagliari in Sardinia, built by the Pisans from 1216 with the reluctant consent of Judge Benedetta of Cagliari. It became a Pisan stronghold and the centre of their control of southern Sardinia, with towers such as those of…

castell-bank.s: The Castell Bank was founded in 1774 by the counts of Castell in Franconia to manage the finances of their small county and lend to its subjects. It survived the county's mediatisation in 1806 and remains in the hands of the family, making it one of the oldest banks in Bavaria.

castro-urdiales.s: Castro Urdiales is a port town on the Bay of Biscay in Cantabria, in northern Spain. It is identified with the Roman colony of Flaviobriga, founded under Vespasian in the territory of the Autrigones.

catalan-company.s: The Catalan Company was a band of mercenaries, mostly Catalan and Aragonese almogavars, led first by Roger de Flor and hired by the Byzantine Empire in 1303 against the Turks. After quarrelling with Byzantium it ravaged Thrace and Macedonia, then defeated and killed Duke…

caterina-sforza.s: Caterina Sforza was the daughter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan, and wife of Girolamo Riario, lord of Imola and Forlì. After her husband's murder in 1488 she ruled the lordship as regent for her son.

caucasus-line-cossack-host.s: The Caucasus Line Cossack Host was formed in 1832 from Cossack regiments settled along the fortified Caucasus Line on the Terek and Kuban rivers. It garrisoned the frontier during the Caucasian War against the mountain peoples.

cecil-calvert.s: Cecil Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, was the English proprietor of the Province of Maryland. Charles I granted the charter to him in 1632 after his father George Calvert's death, and he sent the first settlers in 1634 under his brother Leonard, though he never visited the colony.

cen-chunxuan.s: Cen Chunxuan was a late Qing official who served as governor-general of Sichuan and of Liangguang. In the early Republic he opposed Yuan Shikai, and from 1918 he chaired the directorate of the military government at Canton after the Guangxi generals forced Sun Yat-sen out.

cenel-conaill.s: The Cenél Conaill were a kindred of the northern Uí Néill descended from Conall Gulban, a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages, and based in Tír Chonaill, modern County Donegal. Saint Columba belonged to them.

central-valley-costa-rica.s: The Central Valley is a highland basin in the middle of Costa Rica, containing the cities of San José, Cartago, Heredia and Alajuela. Its fertile volcanic soils and mild climate made it the centre of Spanish settlement and, from the 1830s, of coffee growing, whose exports…

cerro-azul-peru.s: Cerro Azul is a coastal headland and archaeological site in the lower Cañete valley of Peru, south of Lima. In the late pre-Hispanic period it was a fortified fishing centre of the lordship of Guarco, with large adobe buildings for storing and processing fish.

cesare-maria-de-vecchi.s: Cesare Maria De Vecchi was an Italian Fascist leader, one of the quadrumvirs of the March on Rome in 1922. As governor of Italian Somaliland from 1923 to 1928 he conquered the northern sultanates, and as governor of the Italian Aegean Islands from 1936 to 1940 he imposed…

chai-rong.s: Chai Rong, Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou, was the adopted son of its founder Guo Wei and reigned from 954. An able ruler, he reformed the army and finances, suppressed Buddhist monasteries to obtain bronze for coins, and took territory from the Southern Tang and the Khitan Liao.

chand-bibi.s: Chand Bibi was a princess of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate who also served as regent of the Bijapur Sultanate. She is best known for defending the city of Ahmadnagar against the Mughal army of Prince Murad in 1595 to 1596, which forced a treaty.

chand-sultan.s: Chand Sultan was a Gond ruler of the Deogarh kingdom in central India, son of Bakht Buland Shah. He made Nagpur, founded by his father around 1702, his capital and continued the clearing and settlement of new land.

chao-mahaphrom-surathada.s: Chao Mahaphrom Surathada was the last ruling prince of Nan in northern Thailand, succeeding in 1918. By then Siam's provincial reforms had stripped the Nan princes of real authority.

chao-nakhon-nu.s: Chao Nakhon Nu was the governor of Nakhon Si Thammarat in southern Siam who declared himself an independent ruler after the fall of Ayutthaya to the Burmese in 1767. In 1769 Taksin of Thonburi captured the city and took him to Thonburi, but later pardoned him and reinstated…

charles-prince-of-nassau-usingen.s: Charles was Prince of Nassau-Usingen from 1718. In 1744 he moved his residence from Usingen to Biebrich Palace on the Rhine near Wiesbaden, which grew as his capital.

charles-prince-of-isenburg.s: Charles was Prince of Isenburg-Birstein from 1803. In 1806 he joined Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine, gaining full sovereignty and absorbing the lands of the other Isenburg lines, and supplied a regiment to the French army.

charles-brooke-rajah-of-sarawak.s: Charles Brooke was the second White Rajah of Sarawak, succeeding his uncle James Brooke in 1868 after years commanding forts and Iban forces. During a reign of nearly fifty years he greatly enlarged Sarawak at the expense of Brunei, suppressed headhunting and encouraged…

charles-vyner-brooke.s: Charles Vyner Brooke was the third and last White Rajah of Sarawak, ruling from 1917. In 1941 he granted a constitution limiting his powers, shortly before the Japanese occupation.

charles-coghlan.s: Sir Charles Coghlan was a lawyer and politician in Rhodesia who led the campaign against joining the Union of South Africa. After white voters chose responsible government in the 1922 referendum, he became the first premier of the self-governing Colony of Southern Rhodesia in…

charles-de-la-tour.n: Charles de Saint-Étienne de La Tour
charles-de-la-tour.s: Charles de Saint-Étienne de La Tour was a French colonist and fur trader in Acadia. In the 1640s he fought a small civil war with his rival Charles de Menou d'Aulnay over control of the colony, during which d'Aulnay captured his fort on the Saint John River in 1645.

charles-de-montigny.s: Charles de Montigny was a French diplomat, the first French consul in Shanghai from 1847. In 1849 he obtained from the Chinese authorities a concession between the walled city and the British settlement, the origin of the Shanghai French Concession.

charles-de-sales.s: Charles de Sales was a French Knight Hospitaller who succeeded Philippe de Longvilliers de Poincy as governor of the French part of Saint Kitts and the order's Caribbean islands in 1660. He was killed in 1666 fighting the English on Saint Kitts, shortly after the order had…

charles-debbas.s: Charles Debbas was a Lebanese Greek Orthodox lawyer and politician. When the constitution of May 1926 turned Greater Lebanon into the Lebanese Republic under the French Mandate, he was elected its first president, serving until 1934.

charles-iii-of-navarre.s: Charles III the Noble was King of Navarre from 1387, of the French house of Évreux. Unlike his father Charles the Bad, he kept peace with Castile and France, exchanging his Norman claims for the duchy of Nemours.

charles-iii-william-margrave-of-baden-du.n: Charles III William, Margrave of Baden-Durlach
charles-iii-william-margrave-of-baden-du.s: Charles III William was Margrave of Baden-Durlach from 1709. In 1715 he founded the city of Karlsruhe as his new residence, laid out with streets radiating from the palace tower like the ribs of a fan.

charles-la-trobe.s: Charles La Trobe was an English administrator who became superintendent of the Port Phillip District in 1839 and the first lieutenant-governor of the Colony of Victoria when it separated from New South Wales in 1851. Weeks later the gold rush began, and his government…

charles-lawrence.s: Charles Lawrence was a British army officer and governor of Nova Scotia from 1753. Doubting the loyalty of the French-speaking Acadians, he and his council ordered their deportation in 1755, expelling thousands to the British colonies and beyond.

charles-magoon.s: Charles Magoon was an American lawyer and administrator who had governed the Panama Canal Zone. In 1906 he replaced William Howard Taft as provisional governor of Cuba during the second American occupation and ruled until 1909.

charles-ohara.s: Charles O'Hara was a British army officer who served as governor of the Province of Senegambia, Britain's colony on the Senegal and Gambia rivers, from 1765 to 1776, where he was accused of harsh rule and slave trading. In the American Revolutionary War he surrendered the…

charles-the-simple.s: Charles the Simple was a Carolingian King of West Francia, crowned in 893 and sole king from 898. In 911, by the treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, he granted the lands around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo, the origin of the Duchy of Normandy.

charles-theodore-elector-of-bavaria.s: Charles Theodore was a Wittelsbach prince of the Sulzbach line who inherited the Electoral Palatinate in 1742 and the Electorate of Bavaria in 1777. His attempt to exchange Bavaria for the Austrian Netherlands led to the War of the Bavarian Succession.

charles-vii-of-france.s: Charles VII was King of France from 1422. Helped by Joan of Arc, who raised the siege of Orléans and saw him crowned at Reims in 1429, he recovered northern France and Gascony from the English, ending the Hundred Years' War.

charles-viii-of-france.s: Charles VIII was King of France from 1483, governed in his minority by his sister Anne of France and her husband Peter of Bourbon. In 1491 he married Anne of Brittany, bringing the duchy under French control.

charles-woodford.s: Charles Morris Woodford was an English naturalist who explored the Solomon Islands in the 1880s and urged Britain to annex them. In 1896 he became the first Resident Commissioner of the British Solomon Islands Protectorate, setting up the administration at Tulagi.

charles-xiii-of-sweden.s: Charles XIII was King of Sweden from 1809, after the deposition of his nephew Gustav IV Adolf, and King of Norway from November 1814. Childless, he adopted the French marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte as heir.

charles-xiv-john.s: Charles XIV John, born Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, was a French marshal under Napoleon who was elected heir to the Swedish throne in 1810. He joined the coalition against Napoleon and forced Denmark to cede Norway in 1814.

charles-maurice-de-talleyrand.s: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand was a French bishop turned diplomat who served as foreign minister under the Directory, Napoleon and the restored Bourbons. In 1806 Napoleon made him sovereign Prince of Benevento, a former papal enclave in southern Italy, which he governed…

charlotte-amalie.s: Charlotte Amalie is the capital of the United States Virgin Islands, on the island of St Thomas. Founded by the Danish West India Company in the 1670s and named after the Danish queen in 1691, it had a fine natural harbour and became a free port and trading centre of the…

chateau-gaillard.s: Château Gaillard is a ruined castle above the Seine at Les Andelys in Normandy, built in 1196–1198 by Richard I of England to guard the duchy against Philip II of France. After Richard's death Philip besieged it from 1203 and took it in March 1204, opening the way to Rouen.

chaulukya-dynasty.s: The Chaulukya dynasty, also called the Solankis, ruled Gujarat from Anahilapataka (Patan) from about 940 to 1244. Under kings such as Bhima I, Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala it controlled much of western India and patronised Jain and Hindu temples, including the sun…

chen-mingshu.s: Chen Mingshu was a Chinese general from Guangdong and a former commander of the Nineteenth Route Army. Breaking with Chiang Kai-shek, he joined Li Jishen, Cai Tingkai and Jiang Guangnai in proclaiming the Fujian People's Government at Fuzhou in November 1933, which Nationalist…

chen-youliang.s: Chen Youliang was a Chinese rebel leader of the late Yuan period, the son of a fisherman, who rose as an officer in Xu Shouhui's Red Turban regime on the middle Yangtze. In 1360 he killed Xu and proclaimed himself emperor of Han, the state known as Chen Han.

chet-ton-dynasty.s: The Chet Ton dynasty, meaning 'seven princes', was the ruling house of Lampang and Chiang Mai, descended from the seven sons of the Lampang leader Chai Kaeo. Led by Kawila, the brothers joined Siam in driving the Burmese out of Lan Na from 1774 and then governed Chiang Mai,…

chi-lang-pass.s: Chi Lang Pass is a narrow mountain pass in Lang Son province in northern Vietnam, on the main route from China to the Red River delta. Vietnamese forces under Le Hoan defeated a Song invasion there in 981, and in 1427 Le Loi's army ambushed the Ming relief force there, killing…

chiang-rai.s: Chiang Rai is a city in northern Thailand on the Kok River, founded by King Mangrai of Ngoenyang in 1262. It served as Mangrai's base for his expansion southward, which led to the conquest of Hariphunchai in 1292 and the founding of Chiang Mai in 1296 as the capital of Lan Na.

chiang-saen.s: Chiang Saen is an ancient town on the Mekong in the far north of Thailand, near the Golden Triangle where Thailand, Laos and Myanmar meet. Northern Thai chronicles make it the seat of Ngoenyang, the principality of Mangrai's ancestors, before he moved south to found Chiang Rai…

chief-pleas.s: The Chief Pleas is the parliament of Sark in the Channel Islands. It began with the holders of the forty tenements into which Helier de Carteret divided the island when he settled it under a charter from Elizabeth I in 1565.

childeric-i.s: Childeric I was a king of the Salian Franks, traditionally the son of Merovech, who ruled from Tournai until his death around 481. He fought as an ally of Rome against the Visigoths and Saxons on the Loire.

chileshe-chepela.s: Chileshe Chepela was Chitimukulu, the paramount chief of the Bemba of north-eastern Zambia, in the first half of the 19th century. He extended Bemba power by raiding neighbouring peoples and opened trade with Swahili-Arab caravans from the east coast, exchanging ivory and…

chintamanrao-patwardhan.s: Chintamanrao Patwardhan, known as Appa Saheb, was a Maratha chief of the Patwardhan family and the founder of Sangli State. In a division of the family estates in 1782 he separated from the family seat at Miraj and made Sangli his own capital, later building its fort and…

chosokabe-kunichika.s: Chosokabe Kunichika was a Japanese warlord of Tosa province on Shikoku and head of the Chosokabe clan in the Sengoku period. Raised in exile after his father's death in a war among the local families, he recovered the clan castle of Oko and rebuilt Chosokabe power in central…

christian-august-prince-of-anhalt-zerbst.s: Christian August, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, was a German prince and a general in Prussian service who governed Stettin. He became joint ruler of Anhalt-Zerbst with his brother in 1742 and sole prince shortly before his death in 1747.

christian-august-count-palatine-of-sulzb.n: Christian August, Count Palatine of Sulzbach
christian-august-count-palatine-of-sulzb.s: Christian August, Count Palatine of Sulzbach, was the son of Augustus of Palatinate-Sulzbach, a branch of the Wittelsbach family. He gained full sovereignty over Sulzbach in 1656 after a settlement with Palatinate-Neuburg.

christian-ii-of-denmark.s: Christian II of Denmark was king of Denmark and Norway from 1513 and of Sweden from 1520 to 1521, the last monarch of the Kalmar Union to rule all three kingdoms. After reconquering Sweden he had some eighty nobles and clergy executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath of November…

christian-ii-count-palatine-of-zweibruck.n: Christian II, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld
christian-ii-count-palatine-of-zweibruck.s: Christian II, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld, ruled Birkenfeld, a minor branch of the Wittelsbach family, from 1654 until his death in 1717. Through his marriage to Catherine Agathe, heiress of the lords of Rappoltstein, he acquired the lordship of Rappoltstein…

christian-iii-of-denmark.s: Christian III of Denmark was king of Denmark and Norway from 1534 to 1559. He won the throne in the civil war known as the Count's Feud and in 1536 introduced the Lutheran Reformation, seizing the lands of the church and strengthening the crown.

christian-iii-count-palatine-of-zweibruc.n: Christian III, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken
christian-iii-count-palatine-of-zweibruc.s: Christian III, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, was the son of Christian II of Birkenfeld, a minor branch of the Wittelsbach family. In 1731 he inherited the Duchy of Palatinate-Zweibrücken on the extinction of the senior line, and the Birkenfeld branch moved there as…

christoph-bernhard-von-galen.s: Christoph Bernhard von Galen was prince-bishop of Münster from 1650 to 1678. He broke the independence of the city of Münster in 1661 and built a strong standing army, earning the nickname 'Bomben-Bernd' for his use of artillery.

christoph-martin-wieland.s: Christoph Martin Wieland was a German poet and novelist of the Enlightenment, born near Biberach, where he served as town clerk from 1760 to 1769. He translated twenty-two of Shakespeare's plays into German and wrote the novel Geschichte des Agathon and the verse epic Oberon.

cihangiroglu-ibrahim-bey.s: Cihangiroglu Ibrahim Bey was a notable of Kars who headed the Southwestern Caucasian Republic, a short-lived Muslim government set up after Ottoman troops withdrew from the region under the Armistice of Mudros in 1918. His government claimed Kars, Ardahan, Batum and…

cingetorix-cantium.s: Cingetorix was one of four kings who ruled Cantium, modern Kent, when Julius Caesar invaded Britain in 54 BCE. On the orders of Cassivellaunus he and the other kings, Carvilius, Taximagulus and Segovax, attacked the Roman naval camp, but they were driven off.

cingetorix-treveri.s: Cingetorix was a noble of the Treveri, a Gallic people of the Moselle valley, in the 50s BCE. He backed Julius Caesar against his father-in-law Indutiomarus, leader of the anti-Roman faction, and Caesar recognised him as chief of the tribe in 54 BCE.

citarum-river.s: The Citarum River is the longest river in West Java, Indonesia, flowing from the highlands south of Bandung to the Java Sea east of Jakarta. Sundanese tradition, chiefly the Carita Parahyangan, holds that around 669 the lands of Tarumanagara were divided along it, the Sunda…

civita-castellana.s: Civita Castellana is a town in the province of Viterbo in northern Lazio, Italy, built on a tufa plateau above deep ravines. It stands on the site of Falerii, the chief town of the Faliscans, which Rome destroyed in 241 BCE, moving its people to Falerii Novi on the plain.

clifford-dupont.s: Clifford Dupont was a British-born Rhodesian politician and a minister in Ian Smith's government at the Unilateral Declaration of Independence in 1965. Smith appointed him Officer Administering the Government in place of the British governor, and when Rhodesia declared itself…

cocijoeza.s: Cocijoeza was the Zapotec king of Zaachila in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. Around 1490 he conquered the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and moved his seat there, then resisted the Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl in a long siege of the mountain fortress of Guiengola.

columba.s: Columba, or Colm Cille, was an Irish monk of the Cenél Conaill, a branch of the northern Uí Néill, who founded the monastery of Iona off western Scotland around 563. From Iona he and his monks spread Christianity in Dál Riata and among the Picts, and according to his…

commius.s: Commius was a king of the Atrebates of northern Gaul in the 1st century BCE. Installed by Julius Caesar, he served as Caesar's envoy to the Britons in 55 BCE, but joined Vercingetorix's revolt in 52 BCE and later fled to Britain.

company-of-merchants-trading-to-africa.s: The Company of Merchants Trading to Africa was a British association, created by act of Parliament in 1750, that took over the West African forts of the Royal African Company in 1752. Funded by a parliamentary grant, it maintained Cape Coast Castle and other posts on the Gold…

con-oneill-of-clandeboye.s: Con O'Neill of Clandeboye was the last Gaelic lord of Upper Clandeboye in County Down, Ireland. Imprisoned at Carrickfergus in 1602, he escaped with the help of the Scottish laird Hugh Montgomery, who in return obtained a share of his lands.

concepcion-del-uruguay.s: Concepción del Uruguay is a city in Entre Ríos province, Argentina, on the Uruguay River, founded in 1783. In 1815 it hosted the Congress of Oriente, called by José Artigas for the provinces of his Federal League.

concordat-of-worms.s: The Concordat of Worms was the agreement of September 1122 between Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II that ended the Investiture Controversy. The emperor gave up investing bishops with ring and staff, while in Germany elections were to take place in his presence and he…

conference-of-ambassadors.s: The Conference of Ambassadors was a body of the Allied powers set up in Paris in 1920 to enforce and interpret the peace treaties after the First World War. Made up of the ambassadors of Britain, Italy and Japan under a French chair, it settled frontier questions: in November…

congalach-cnogba.s: Congalach Cnogba was king of Brega and high king of Ireland from 944 until his death in 956, the last of the Síl nÁedo Sláine to hold the kingship of Tara. Named after Knowth (Cnogba) in the Boyne valley, he sacked Viking Dublin in 944.

congress-of-angostura.s: The Congress of Angostura was the assembly convened by Simón Bolívar at Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar, on the Orinoco, which opened in February 1819. Bolívar's address set out his ideas on republican government, and the congress elected him president of Venezuela.

conn-bacach-oneill.s: Conn Bacach O'Neill was king of Tír Eoghain from 1519 and the first Earl of Tyrone. Under Henry VIII's policy of surrender and regrant he submitted in 1542, gave up the title of The O'Neill and received an English earldom.

conrad-ii-of-znojmo.s: Conrad II of Znojmo was a Přemyslid prince who ruled the Moravian appanage of Znojmo in the 12th century. He led the Moravian princes who challenged Duke Vladislaus II for the Bohemian throne, besieging Prague in 1142.

conrad-iii-otto.s: Conrad III Otto was a Přemyslid prince of Znojmo and Brno whom Emperor Frederick Barbarossa made margrave of Moravia in 1182, holding the land directly from the empire. In 1189 he became Duke of Bohemia, reuniting Moravia with Bohemia, and issued the Statuta Conradi, a code of…

conrad-the-red.s: Conrad the Red was duke of Lotharingia from 944, a Franconian noble of the Salian family who married Liutgard, daughter of Otto I. In 953 he joined the rebellion of Otto's son Liudolf and lost his duchy.

continuation-war.s: The Continuation War was the conflict between Finland and the Soviet Union from June 1941 to September 1944, fought alongside Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union. Finland recovered the lands lost in the Winter War and occupied much of Soviet Karelia, including Petrozavodsk.

contrebia-belaisca.s: Contrebia Belaisca was a Celtiberian town of the Belli at Cabezo de las Minas, near Botorrita south of Zaragoza in Spain. Excavations there found the Botorrita bronzes, the longest known texts in the Celtiberian language, and a Latin bronze tablet of 87 BCE recording a Roman…

convention-of-moss.s: The Convention of Moss was the ceasefire agreement signed on 14 August 1814 at Moss, south of Christiania, that ended the brief Swedish–Norwegian War. Norway's regent Christian Frederik agreed to abdicate, while Sweden accepted the Norwegian constitution of 17 May 1814.

coptic-orthodox-church.s: The Coptic Orthodox Church is the main Christian church of Egypt, headed by the Pope of Alexandria. It rejected the Council of Chalcedon in 451 and became separate from the imperial church, and most Egyptians followed it until Islam gradually spread after the Arab conquest.

corazon-aquino.s: Corazon Aquino was president of the Philippines from 1986 to 1992, the first woman to hold the office. The widow of the opposition leader Benigno Aquino Jr., murdered in 1983, she challenged Ferdinand Marcos in the 1986 snap election, and the People Power Revolution drove…

cormac-mac-carthaigh.s: Cormac Mac Carthaigh was king of Desmond, and at times of all Munster, from about 1123 until his murder in 1138. A rival of the O'Briens of Thomond, he ruled from Cork and Cashel and supported reform of the Irish church.

cornelis-gooyer.s: Cornelis Gooyer was the first Dutch commander of Mauritius, sent by the Dutch East India Company in 1638 to set up a permanent post at Grand Port in the south-east of the island. With a small garrison he cut ebony for export and supplied passing ships, but the settlement…

cornelis-jol.s: Cornelis Jol, nicknamed Houtebeen ('Peg Leg'), was a Dutch admiral and privateer of the Dutch West India Company. After years of raiding Spanish and Portuguese shipping in the Caribbean, he led the fleet that captured Luanda from the Portuguese in August 1641 and then took São…

cornelis-speelman.s: Cornelis Speelman was a Dutch East India Company commander and governor-general of the Dutch East Indies from 1681 to 1684. Allied with Arung Palakka of Bone, he defeated Sultan Hasanuddin of Gowa and imposed the Treaty of Bongaya of 1667, which ended Makassar's power and its…

cosimo-i-de-medici.s: Cosimo I de' Medici became duke of Florence at seventeen after the murder of his cousin Alessandro in 1537. He crushed the republican exiles at Montemurlo, conquered Siena in the 1550s with Spanish backing and built a centralised state, commissioning the Uffizi from Giorgio…

council-of-elvira.s: The Council of Elvira was a synod of the church in Roman Hispania held at Iliberris (Elvira), near modern Granada, in the early 4th century, usually dated around 305. Its 81 canons, among the earliest surviving church laws, dealt with idolatry, marriage and relations with Jews…

council-of-lithuania.s: The Council of Lithuania, or Taryba, was the body elected by the Vilnius Conference in September 1917, under German occupation, to represent Lithuania. Chaired by Antanas Smetona, it signed the Act of Independence on 16 February 1918, and in July 1918 briefly proclaimed a…

county-clare.s: County Clare is a county in the west of Ireland, between the Shannon estuary and Galway Bay. It was formed from the Gaelic kingdom of Thomond, ruled by the O'Briens, when the English administration shired the area in the 1570s.

county-leitrim.s: County Leitrim is a county in the north-west of Ireland, on the upper Shannon. It corresponds roughly to West Breifne, the lordship of the O'Rourkes, which the English administration shired as Leitrim in the 1580s after the O'Rourkes' defeat.

court-of-policy.s: The Court of Policy was the governing council of the Dutch colonies of Essequibo and Demerara and later of British Guiana. Made up of officials and representatives of the planters, it shared power with the governor or commander and made local laws.

crazy-horse.s: Crazy Horse was an Oglala Lakota war leader who resisted American expansion onto the northern Plains. He fought in Red Cloud's War, at the Rosebud and, alongside Sitting Bull, in the defeat of George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn in June 1876.

cristobal-arnaldo-ysasi.s: Cristóbal Arnaldo Ysasi was the last Spanish governor of Jamaica. After the English captured the island in 1655 he led a guerrilla resistance from the mountains with the help of free Africans, while expeditions from Cuba tried to retake it.

cristobal-mendoza.s: Cristóbal Mendoza was a Venezuelan lawyer and the first holder of executive power in independent Venezuela, as a member of the triumvirate created in March 1811. After the fall of the First Republic he worked with Simón Bolívar, who named him governor of Caracas in 1813.

constans-ii.s: Constans II was Byzantine emperor from 641 to 668, during the Arab conquests that took Egypt and threatened Anatolia. He moved his court west in 663, campaigned against the Lombards in southern Italy and resided at Syracuse in Sicily, strengthening Byzantine positions there,…

chipata.s: Chipata, called Fort Jameson until 1970, is a town in eastern Zambia near the Malawi border. It was founded by the British South Africa Company around 1899 after the defeat of Mpezeni's Ngoni kingdom and named after Leander Starr Jameson.

cividale-del-friuli.s: Cividale del Friuli is a town in north-eastern Italy founded by Julius Caesar as Forum Iulii, from which the region of Friuli takes its name. In 568 the Lombard king Alboin left his nephew Gisulf there as the first Lombard duke in Italy.

castle-of-grand-magne.s: The Castle of Grand Magne was a fortress built around 1248 by William II of Villehardouin, Prince of Achaea, on the Mani peninsula in the southern Peloponnese, to control the local Slavs and Maniots. After his capture at the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259, William ceded it with…

cizre.s: Cizre, known in Arabic as Jazirat ibn Umar, is a town on the Tigris in south-eastern Turkey, near the borders of Syria and Iraq. In the 12th and 13th centuries it was ruled by a branch of the Zengid dynasty.

conquest-of-the-desert.s: The Conquest of the Desert was the Argentine military campaign, led by General Julio Argentino Roca from 1878 to 1879 and continued until 1885, that seized the pampas and northern Patagonia from Mapuche, Tehuelche and other indigenous peoples. Thousands were killed or…

constantine-i-of-greece.s: Constantine I was King of Greece from 1913 to 1917 and from 1920 to 1922. A successful commander in the Balkan Wars, he insisted on neutrality in the First World War, which brought him into conflict with Eleftherios Venizelos and led to the National Schism.

county-offaly.s: County Offaly is a county in the Irish midlands. It was created in 1556 under Mary I, when the lands of the O'Connor Faly of Uí Failge and neighbouring territories were shired and planted with English settlers as King's County, named after Mary's husband Philip, with Daingean…

caucasus-army-of-islam.s: The Caucasus Army of Islam was an Ottoman force formed in 1918 under Nuri Pasha, combining Ottoman troops with Azerbaijani volunteers, to advance into the South Caucasus after Russia's collapse. It defeated the forces of the Baku Commune and then of the Centrocaspian…

chaktomuk.s: Chaktomuk, 'four faces', called Quatre Bras by the French, is the meeting of waters at Phnom Penh where the Mekong joins the Tonle Sap and divides into the Mekong and Bassac channels. After the court left Angkor in the 15th century, the confluence became the heart of the…

cidade-velha.s: Cidade Velha, originally Ribeira Grande, on the island of Santiago, was the first capital of Portuguese Cape Verde and one of the first European towns in the tropics. It became a major entrepot of the Atlantic slave trade between West Africa and the Americas.

catherine-cornaro.s: Catherine Cornaro was a Venetian noblewoman who became queen of Cyprus by marrying King James II, of the Lusignan dynasty, in 1472. After the deaths of her husband in 1473 and their infant son James III in 1474, she reigned as queen, with Venice controlling her government.
